kahf.x:
In an old, old city, the people bowed down to idols made of stone — idols that could not hear a prayer or keep away any harm.

In that city lived a few young men. They stood on the hill and watched their people bowing down, and they knew: this is not a Lord.

And in their hearts was a light that no one knew about.

At night they climbed up to the rooftop and sat in a row, looking at the stars.

They said, "Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth. We will never call upon any god besides Him."

They said it in a whisper, because their king was a cruel tyrant who hurt anyone who disagreed with him.

When the city became too hard for them, they left it at sunset. They carried no food and no money — only their faith.

Seven young men walking down the road, and their dog following them, never leaving their side.

Whoever goes out for the sake of Allah never goes out alone.

They walked as the night came closer, until they reached a huge mountain at the edge of the valley.

At its foot was a wide, dark cave. They stood before it, looking so small beneath it.

They said, "This is our shelter, and our Lord is with us."

They stood at its entrance and raised their hands, with the light in front of them and the darkness behind them:

«ربَّنا آتِنا من لدنك رحمةً وهيِّئْ لنا من أمرنا رَشَداً» (Our Lord, grant us mercy from Yourself, and guide us rightly in our affair.)

One single du'a — and Allah did not turn it away.

Then they went in and fell asleep: seven of them, and the eighth was their dog.

Allah sealed their ears, so they heard nothing and did not wake up.

Their dog lay with his front legs stretched out at the entrance, as if he were guarding them while they knew nothing.

When the sun rose, it turned away from their cave to the right, and when it set, it passed them by on the left.

So its heat never touched them, while they lay in a wide open space inside the cave, with fresh air and shade.

Allah made the sun itself guard them.

The nights went by. New moons rose and disappeared. Grass and flowers grew over the path they had walked on.

Three hundred years, and nine more.

And they were still asleep, as if they had slept for only one day.

Then Allah woke them, and they got up as if nothing had happened. One of them asked, "How long have we stayed here?" They said, "A day, or part of a day."

They were hungry, so they sent one of them to the city to buy food.

He walked into a market where he knew no one, and no one knew him.

When he handed the seller his coins, the people were amazed: "These are from a time long, long ago!"

They followed him all the way to the cave, and that day they learned that Allah's promise is true, and that the One who made them sleep is able to bring people back to life after they die.

Whoever is mindful of Allah, Allah protects him.

📖 Their story is in Surat Al-Kahf.

qarya.x:
A man was travelling alone on a long road, riding his donkey. He had brought food and drink for the day: some dates wrapped in a cloth, a loaf of bread, and a waterskin.

The sun was sinking toward sunset, and the road was empty except for pebbles and the tracks of the wind. His only company was the sound of his donkey's hooves on the stones.

He did not know — as he went along on a day like any other — that today Allah would show him a sign that no one had ever seen before.

When he reached a town on his way, he found it completely in ruins: broken walls, roofs that had fallen in on the people inside, and open doors that led to no one.

There was no sound and no movement. Only the wind, coming in through one gap and going out through another, stirring up the dust and then falling still.

The man stopped on his donkey and looked. And in his heart was a question bigger than the whole town.

He looked at the houses that had turned to dust, and at the old bones under the rubble, white from the long years that had passed over them, and he said to himself:

﴿أَنَّىٰ يُحْيِي هَٰذِهِ اللَّهُ بَعْدَ مَوْتِهَا﴾

He did not say it out of denial or disbelief, but out of wonder: how could these ruins come back to life as they were, with houses and people and voices?

Allah heard his question, and He wanted to show him the answer.

So Allah caused him to die right there, in that very hour, as he stood there wondering.

Everything became still: the man, his donkey standing beside him, the cloth of food on the stone, and the waterskin. The sun set, then rose, then set, then rose.

He felt none of it. Whoever Allah has caused to die does not count the days.

The years passed over the ruined town and over the man.

The rain came and grew green grass between the stones; then the grass dried and turned yellow, then came back again. Birds flew over the ruins a thousand times, built their nests there and left, and others came, built, and left.

A whole hundred years. The man lay sleeping, knowing nothing, and his donkey beside him had become bones.

Then Allah brought him back to life, and he got up as if he had woken from a short nap after noon.

He was asked: ﴿كَمْ لَبِثْتَ﴾

He looked at the sun and saw it had moved only a little from where he had left it, so he thought not even a full day had passed, and he said: ﴿لَبِثْتُ يَوْمًا أَوْ بَعْضَ يَوْمٍ﴾

But the answer was more amazing than anything he had imagined.

﴿بَل لَّبِثْتَ مِائَةَ عَامٍ﴾

A hundred years had passed over him without his feeling them. In that time, people were born, grew up, and died. The roads, the faces, and the names all changed, and everyone he had known was now dust under the ground.

Yet he was just as he had been — not a single hair of him had changed. Time, which wears people away, cannot wear away someone Allah has protected.

Then he was told: ﴿فَانظُرْ إِلَىٰ طَعَامِكَ وَشَرَابِكَ لَمْ يَتَسَنَّهْ﴾

He looked at his cloth bundle, and there were the dates, still soft just as he had left them. The bread had not gone stale, and the water in the skin was clear, its taste and smell unchanged. A hundred years, and nothing had spoiled.

The One who kept his food from spoiling is able to keep its owner from passing away.

﴿وَانظُرْ إِلَىٰ حِمَارِكَ﴾ — He turned, and there was his donkey: white bones scattered on the dust, so spread apart that you could not tell its head from its legs.

Then he watched as the bones rose up and joined one another, each in its place. Then flesh covered them little by little, until the donkey stood up alive on its legs, braying just as before.

He saw with his own eyes what he had asked about in his heart.

When the whole matter became clear to him, he did not say many words. He said one sentence that held everything:

﴿أَعْلَمُ أَنَّ اللَّهَ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ﴾

He had asked a question in his heart, and Allah showed him the answer in his food, in his donkey, and — before them both — in himself.

The One who gives life to old bones after a hundred years will give life to all people on the Day of Judgement.

📖 His story is in Surat Al-Baqarah, verse 259.

qarun.x:
Among the Children of Israel was a man named Qarun. He was one of their own people, from their own families. He walked their streets, and even their little ones knew him.

Then Allah gave him wealth like no one else in the city had: a house that rose above all the other houses, and storerooms full of more than anyone could count.

﴿إِنَّ قَارُونَ كَانَ مِن قَوْمِ مُوسَىٰ فَبَغَىٰ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ — He was one of them, and then he set himself above them.

His storerooms had so many keys that just carrying the keys was heavy for a group of strong men.

﴿مَا إِنَّ مَفَاتِحَهُ لَتَنُوءُ بِالْعُصْبَةِ أُولِي الْقُوَّةِ﴾

Only the keys — not the gold behind them! If carrying the keys tired out strong men, how much was behind the doors?

If he had been thankful, it would have been better for him. But he began to look down on people, seeing himself above them and them beneath him.

He would pass by a needy person standing at his door and not even turn his head. He was asked, and he did not give. He was reminded, and he turned away and walked on. His storerooms grew fuller, but his door never opened for anyone.

Wealth does not ruin a person by itself — it ruins him when it makes him forget the One who gave it.

So the good people among his tribe came to speak to him gently. They were not jealous of him and did not want his money; they were worried for him.

They stood before him in the courtyard of his house and told him one thing: ﴿لَا تَفْرَحْ ۖ إِنَّ اللَّهَ لَا يُحِبُّ الْفَرِحِينَ﴾

Being happy with a blessing is not a sin — the wrong kind of joy is the one that makes a person arrogant, proud, and forgetful of being thankful.

Then they showed him the whole way in just a few words:

﴿وَابْتَغِ فِيمَا آتَاكَ اللَّهُ الدَّارَ الْآخِرَةَ وَلَا تَنسَ نَصِيبَكَ مِنَ الدُّنْيَا وَأَحْسِن كَمَا أَحْسَنَ اللَّهُ إِلَيْكَ﴾

They did not tell him, "Give up your wealth." They said: eat and enjoy it, give some of it away, and let it leave something good behind you that lasts.

But he would not listen. He lifted his head and said one sentence full of all his pride:

﴿إِنَّمَا أُوتِيتُهُ عَلَىٰ عِلْمٍ عِندِي﴾

Meaning: "I earned it with my own knowledge and cleverness, and I owe it to no one."

He forgot that the One who gave it to him can take it away, and that before him there were nations stronger than he was and richer, and none of that helped them at all.

Then he wanted to show people everything he had, so one day he went out to them in his very finest.

﴿فَخَرَجَ عَلَىٰ قَوْمِهِ فِي زِينَتِهِ﴾

A procession that filled the road from wall to wall: decorated animals, clothes shining in the sun, and servants walking all around him. People stood on both sides, watching in silence.

He went out to be seen — not to give.

When some of the people saw him, they wished they could be in his place, and they said as they watched:

﴿يَا لَيْتَ لَنَا مِثْلَ مَا أُوتِيَ قَارُونُ إِنَّهُ لَذُو حَظٍّ عَظِيمٍ﴾

They looked only at the glitter and thought it was great good fortune, and they did not see what lay behind it.

Whoever looks only at the outside of people may wish for something that, if he knew how it ended, he would ask Allah to protect him from.

But some people are not fooled by glitter. They were people whom Allah had given knowledge. They watched the procession pass right in front of them, and their hearts did not stir; not one of them wished to be in his place.

They said: ﴿ثَوَابُ اللَّهِ خَيْرٌ لِّمَنْ آمَنَ وَعَمِلَ صَالِحًا﴾

They did not say it out of jealousy or because they could not have it — they simply saw what the others did not see.

Then the command came, in a moment no one expected.

﴿فَخَسَفْنَا بِهِ وَبِدَارِهِ الْأَرْضَ﴾

The earth split open beneath him, and down he went — he, his palace, his treasures, and his keys — until nothing of him was left above the ground.

Neither his servants nor his money could save him. ﴿فَمَا كَانَ لَهُ مِن فِئَةٍ يَنصُرُونَهُ مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ﴾

The next morning, people found the place where the palace had stood was flat dust with no trace left, as if no building had ever been there.

And those who had wished the day before to be in his place stood looking and saying:

﴿لَوْلَا أَن مَّنَّ اللَّهُ عَلَيْنَا لَخَسَفَ بِنَا﴾

How quickly their wish turned into thanking Allah that it had not come true!

And the words that close the whole story remain:

﴿تِلْكَ الدَّارُ الْآخِرَةُ نَجْعَلُهَا لِلَّذِينَ لَا يُرِيدُونَ عُلُوًّا فِي الْأَرْضِ وَلَا فَسَادًا ۖ وَالْعَاقِبَةُ لِلْمُتَّقِينَ﴾

The Home of the Hereafter is not for those with the most money, but for those who did not seek to rise above other people.

📖 His story is in Surat Al-Qasas, verses 76–83.

qatil.x:
There was once a man who had killed ninety-nine people. He could not count how many homes he had made dark, or how many mothers he had made cry.

Then one day he sat alone in an empty land, and he felt a weight in his chest heavier than his back could carry. He asked himself a question he had never asked before: "Will I stay like this until I die?"

The first step on the right path is for a person to know that he is lost.

So he went out asking: "Who is the most knowledgeable person on earth?"

He stopped people in their streets and markets and asked. He did not hide what he had done, and he did not make his number even one less. People moved away from him; they pointed him somewhere and then hurried off.

He was sent to a monk in a little hermitage outside the village, who worshipped there and kept away from everyone.

He was not looking for someone to make him feel better — he was looking for someone to show him a way out.

He climbed up to the monk and said, "I have killed ninety-nine people. Can I still repent?"

The monk looked at him and was horrified by the number. He did not judge the matter with knowledge, but only by the fear in his heart, and he said, "No."

One small word — and it slammed shut in a man's face a door that Allah has opened for all His servants.

The man heard it and fell silent. He had not asked for much — just one word that would leave him a little bit of hope.

But the word he got closed instead of opening, and he stood there seeing no road ahead of him. Despair took the place of hope, and the man went back to what he used to be, even worse than before.

Whoever makes a person lose hope in Allah's mercy has wronged that person — and himself.

So he killed the monk too, and with him he reached a full hundred.

Then he left the hermitage alone. Its door stood open behind him with no one inside. The road ahead was as he had left it, and the land was the same; nothing had changed.

It gave him no rest and no relief — it only added weight to his weight.

But he did not stop asking. And that is what is amazing about him.

He could have said, "I asked, and I was refused, so there is no repentance for me." But he asked again.

A second time he asked who was the most knowledgeable person on earth, and in his eyes was something that had not been there the first time: a man with a heavy load who did not want to die the way he was, and who would not accept that answer.

Whoever does not stop asking has already found the door half open.

He was sent to a man of true knowledge. He came to him and told him everything, mentioning the hundred without leaving out a single one.

The scholar was not horrified and did not panic. He simply looked at him and said, "And who could stand between you and repentance?"

One question brought the man back to life. The One who forgives does not keep count the way people do, and a door that Allah has opened, no servant can close.

And the scholar did not leave him with just words; he showed him what to do:

"Go to such-and-such a land, for there are people there who worship Allah. Worship Allah with them, and do not go back to your own land, for it is a land of evil."

He did not tell him, "You feel sorry, and that is enough." He told him: move, change your companions, and do good deeds with good people.

Repentance is a word followed by a road, and regret followed by action.

He set off that very day without looking back. He left his home, his family, and everyone he knew, and went toward a land he had never seen, where he knew no one.

A long road between two lands: one behind him, holding everything he had done, and one ahead of him with nothing of his past in it. Between them, only pebbles, wind, and a road that seemed never to end.

Whoever sets out seeking to be saved does not care how far he has to walk.

When he had gone halfway, death came to him.

He fell in an empty land, with no village to his right or his left, and no one who knew about him or passed by. He died on the road, before reaching where he was going, before doing a single good deed in the land of the righteous.

So a person who dies on the road to goodness — is he counted among those who arrived, or among those who never set out at all?

The angels disagreed about him when he died. Some said, "He set out repenting, turning to Allah with his heart." Others said, "He never did a single good deed."

It was decided between them that they should measure the distance to the land he had left and to the land he was heading for. Whichever one he was closer to, he would belong to its people.

They measured, and they found him closer to the land he was heading for — by just one hand-span. So he belonged to its people.

His soul was taken to the land he had wanted, and he was forgiven.

A hundred lives, and a man who died on the road before doing even one good deed in the land of the righteous — and he was forgiven, because he set out and did not sit still.

So never say, "My sin is too big to be forgiven." The door stays open as long as there is life left.

📖 His story is in Sahih Muslim, in the Book of Repentance.

jannatayn.x:
There were two men. Allah gave one of them two gardens, and the other was not given anything like them.

﴿جَعَلْنَا لِأَحَدِهِمَا جَنَّتَيْنِ مِنْ أَعْنَابٍ وَحَفَفْنَاهُمَا بِنَخْلٍ وَجَعَلْنَا بَيْنَهُمَا زَرْعًا﴾

Two vineyards surrounded on every side by palm trees, with green crops growing between them. A perfect garden, missing nothing.

They were not like other people's gardens, which give fruit one year and fail the next.

﴿كِلْتَا الْجَنَّتَيْنِ آتَتْ أُكُلَهَا وَلَمْ تَظْلِم مِّنْهُ شَيْئًا وَفَجَّرْنَا خِلَالَهُمَا نَهَرًا﴾

They gave everything they had and held nothing back, and a river ran between them that never stopped, so their owner never had to fear thirst.

All of this was a gift; none of it came from his own earning.

The man saw the bunches of grapes hanging from the trellises, so heavy they almost touched the ground. He could not count them, and he never worried about a bad year.

﴿وَكَانَ لَهُ ثَمَرٌ﴾

But he looked at them with a look that was not a thankful one. He saw them as the fruit of his own hands, his own ideas, and his own planning, and he forgot the One who made them grow.

The beginning of arrogance is giving credit to someone who does not deserve it.

He had a friend who had less money and fewer children than him. He would meet him on the road, talk with him, and walk with him.

While they were talking, he said to him: ﴿أَنَا أَكْثَرُ مِنكَ مَالًا وَأَعَزُّ نَفَرًا﴾

He did not say it as a joke. He said it because he thought money and children were a scale for weighing people, and he saw himself on one side of the scale and his friend on the other.

Whoever weighs people by what is in their hands is using the wrong scale.

﴿وَدَخَلَ جَنَّتَهُ وَهُوَ ظَالِمٌ لِّنَفْسِهِ﴾

He walked in among the trellises like an owner, with shade above him and water at his feet, and the grape bunches brushing his shoulder as he passed.

His wrong was not that he owned it — it was that he went in and did not remember who had given it to him.

He entered it with his eyes, but not with his heart. It was in his hands, but not in his thanks.

﴿قَالَ مَا أَظُنُّ أَن تَبِيدَ هَٰذِهِ أَبَدًا﴾

These were the words of a man who had never seen anything disappear, so he thought nothing ever would. He looked at the green all around him, and at the water that never stopped, and he thought it would last like the mountains, never knowing dryness or an end.

But what people think is firm is only held up by Allah's command — and if He lets it go, it falls in a single night.

Then he said even more: ﴿وَمَا أَظُنُّ السَّاعَةَ قَائِمَةً وَلَئِن رُّدِدتُّ إِلَىٰ رَبِّي لَأَجِدَنَّ خَيْرًا مِّنْهَا مُنقَلَبًا﴾

Meaning: "If there is a resurrection — and I do not think there is — He will give me something even better there than what I have here."

He thought being rich was a sign that Allah was pleased with him, and that whatever he was given here he would be given there. But that is not how it is shared out.

His friend did not keep quiet, and he did not flatter him just because he was richer.

﴿قَالَ لَهُ صَاحِبُهُ وَهُوَ يُحَاوِرُهُ أَكَفَرْتَ بِالَّذِي خَلَقَكَ مِن تُرَابٍ ثُمَّ مِن نُّطْفَةٍ ثُمَّ سَوَّاكَ رَجُلًا﴾

He reminded him of where he began: dust, then a tiny drop, then a complete man.

Whoever knows where he came from will never be arrogant toward anyone.

Then he said words that he stood firm on all alone, with no money and no people behind him:

﴿لَّٰكِنَّا هُوَ اللَّهُ رَبِّي وَلَا أُشْرِكُ بِرَبِّي أَحَدًا﴾

The poor man said it right to the rich man's face, in his garden and among his trellises, with nothing in his hand to lose and nothing to hope to gain.

True honour is not having something to show off. It is saying the truth when you have nothing at all.

Then he showed him the words he should have said when he entered:

﴿وَلَوْلَا إِذْ دَخَلْتَ جَنَّتَكَ قُلْتَ مَا شَاءَ اللَّهُ لَا قُوَّةَ إِلَّا بِاللَّهِ﴾

Two short phrases that do not tire the tongue. If he had said them when he saw all that green, it would have been kept safe for him.

Nothing protects a blessing like giving the credit to the One it comes from.

﴿إِن تَرَنِ أَنَا أَقَلَّ مِنكَ مَالًا وَوَلَدًا﴾

﴿فَعَسَىٰ رَبِّي أَن يُؤْتِيَنِ خَيْرًا مِّن جَنَّتِكَ وَيُرْسِلَ عَلَيْهَا حُسْبَانًا مِّنَ السَّمَاءِ فَتُصْبِحَ صَعِيدًا زَلَقًا﴾

﴿أَوْ يُصْبِحَ مَاؤُهَا غَوْرًا فَلَن تَسْتَطِيعَ لَهُ طَلَبًا﴾

He did not pray against him; he only reminded him that the matter was not in his hands.

Then came what he had never expected.

﴿وَأُحِيطَ بِثَمَرِهِ فَأَصْبَحَ يُقَلِّبُ كَفَّيْهِ عَلَىٰ مَا أَنفَقَ فِيهَا وَهِيَ خَاوِيَةٌ عَلَىٰ عُرُوشِهَا﴾

In the morning, the vines had collapsed onto their trellises, the palm trees were broken, the crops were crushed straw, and the stream was dry.

The man who had said "it will never perish" saw it perish in one night.

He stood among what was left of it, turning his hands over: opening them and closing them, looking at them, and nothing was in them. Everything he had spent was gone, and everything he had gathered lay under the fallen trellises.

﴿يَا لَيْتَنِي لَمْ أُشْرِكْ بِرَبِّي أَحَدًا﴾

He said it when it could no longer help him — it had been said to him before, and he had not listened.

The heaviest words on the heart are: "If only I had…"

﴿وَلَمْ تَكُن لَّهُ فِئَةٌ يَنصُرُونَهُ مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ وَمَا كَانَ مُنتَصِرًا﴾

No money to bring it back, no people to help, and nothing he could do.

﴿هُنَالِكَ الْوَلَايَةُ لِلَّهِ الْحَقِّ هُوَ خَيْرٌ ثَوَابًا وَخَيْرٌ عُقْبًا﴾

📖 Their story is in Surat Al-Kahf, verses 32–44.

shiraa.x:
Salim, Rashid, and Hamdan had fished together in the same boat for more years than they could remember.

One morning they went down to the sea before dawn. They pushed the boat off the sand while the sea was calm and the other boats were still on the shore.

They did not talk much; each of them knew his place and went to it: Salim to the rudder — the wooden handle that steers the boat — Rashid to the rope, and Hamdan to the front of the boat to watch the water.

When the wind came, the sail filled up, and the boat leaned on its side and moved forward.

Salim held the rudder, Rashid pulled the rope, and Hamdan pointed them to the deep water. Their hands moved together as if they were one hand, without any of them saying a word to the others.

And so they passed all the other boats, one after another, until their sail was the first thing you could see from the shore.

Then Hamdan said, without meaning anything by it, "If I held the rudder, we'd be faster."

Salim raised his head but did not answer. Rashid said, "And I've been pulling this rope since dawn, and nobody has thanked me."

It was a small remark. Hamdan said it and then forgot it. But it stayed in the hearts of his two friends, and it opened a door between the three of them that had never been open before.

Then they fell silent, but the silence did not put out what was burning in their hearts.

Each one began counting what he had done and forgetting what the other two had done. Rashid saw only the rope in his hand, Salim saw only the rudder, and Hamdan thought the boat would never have moved without his eyes on the water.

The longer the silence lasted, the bigger each one's work grew in his own eyes, and the smaller his friends' work became.

Then what was in their hearts came out through their hands.

Salim turned the rudder a little to the right. Rashid thought he had made a mistake, so he pulled the rope to the left to fix it. When Hamdan saw that, he shouted at both of them to stop.

Now there were three hands in the boat, each trying to take it a different way. But there was only one boat, and it could not go three ways at once.

And the sail twisted.

A moment before, it had been tight and full of wind. Now it shook and flapped, then went slack and hung from the mast like a wet shirt. The rope that Rashid had been pulling with all his strength swung loose and empty.

And so the wind went out of the sail. No one took it from them — they let it slip away while they were quarrelling.

Then the boat stood still.

No wind pushed it and no hand moved it. It rocked with the waves, right and left, and came back to where it was, with the wide sea all around and no shore in sight.

It had not stopped because the wind had died — the other boats were sailing in the very same wind. It had stopped because the three men in it were no longer three together.

While they sat there, the boats that had been behind them sailed past.

They went by one after another, their sails full and their crews working in silence, until they became tiny dots at the edge of the sea and then disappeared. No one even turned to look at them.

Salim, Rashid, and Hamdan watched them go, and they knew that an hour ago they had been the first boat — and that they had stopped their own boat with their own hands.

They sat there so long that they grew tired of the silence.

Rashid held out the end of the rope to Hamdan, without saying anything or looking at his face. Hamdan took it, and he did not say anything either. Salim went back to the rudder and held it the way he held it every day.

None of them said a word of apology. But one hand reached out, and another hand took it, and that was enough.

The rudder straightened, the rope was pulled tight, the wind filled the sail once again, and the boat moved on.

﴿وَلَا تَنَازَعُوا فَتَفْشَلُوا وَتَذْهَبَ رِيحُكُمْ﴾

The "wind" in this ayah means your strength, not the wind in a sail. But Salim, Rashid, and Hamdan saw with their own eyes how it goes away.

📖 Al-Anfal 46, revealed about standing together in ranks before battle. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

shah.x:
Hill Village and Spring Village sat on the two sides of the same valley, with a path between them that people walked every morning and evening.

The people of the two villages traded salt, ropes, and news, and their boys grazed their sheep on the same hillside. There was no hostility between them — only some old words that most had forgotten, and a few had not.

One autumn evening, Nayef came back from the pasture with his sheep. He counted them at the pen and found one missing.

He counted them a second time and a third, and each time one was missing. So he went back to the hillside to look for it until night fell, then returned to the village with nothing but the news.

Until that hour, the whole matter was just a sheep that had lost its way.

When people heard the news, Mas'ud, who was sitting with them, said, "At sunset I saw someone near the pasture. I think he was from Spring Village."

Mas'ud was not lying. He had seen a faraway shape in the last of the light; he could not make out its face or its clothes. But he thought his words would help Nayef find his sheep.

And not one of those sitting there asked him, "Are you sure?"

Then Mas'ud's words left the gathering and walked through the alleys, changing each time they passed from one mouth to another.

The first said, "Mas'ud saw someone." The second said, "He saw them near the sheep." The third said, "He saw them taking it." And the fourth said, "They've been doing this for ages."

None of them lied on purpose, but each one added a little of his own to what he had heard.

That night the men of the village gathered in the square, with a fire between them and their voices getting louder.

Old Sheikh Hamid said, "The path to them is short. We'll go in the morning and ask them. If the sheep is with them, they'll give it back." Someone answered him, "And do you really think they'll admit it?" Sheikh Hamid went quiet and did not say it again.

The truth was only half an hour away, on a path they all knew — yet they did not walk to it to ask.

When daylight came, they set out.

They went down the path into the valley with their shepherd's sticks in their hands, their faces turned toward Spring Village. None of them spoke, and none looked at the man beside him.

Each one thought he was going to take back what was his. Not one of them imagined he was going to wrong people he had never even asked.

When they reached the middle of the valley, they saw a group coming from Spring Village. They stopped, and the others stopped too.

The people coming toward them were carrying a sheep… Nayef's very own sheep! They had found it at dawn in a narrow ravine, recognised its mark, and set out right away to bring it back to its owners.

Suddenly the sticks in the hands of the Hill Village men felt heavier than before.

No one said anything.

The men of Hill Village lowered their sticks to the ground one by one and bowed their heads. Mas'ud stared at his feet and did not lift his head, for now he knew that his words were what had brought them out of their homes.

How hard it is to say "we thought…" after marching out with your stick against people who never wronged you!

Then a man from Spring Village held out the sheep to Nayef, and he took it.

No one asked anyone anything, and no one explained. The people of Spring Village never found out why these men had come out to them with sticks. Each group went back the way it had come, with the sheep trotting in front of Nayef as if nothing had happened.

All of this could have been avoided with one single question — and they never asked it.

And the path between Hill Village and Spring Village stayed as it was, walked by people every morning and evening.

﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا إِن جَاءَكُمْ فَاسِقٌ بِنَبَإٍ فَتَبَيَّنُوا أَن تُصِيبُوا قَوْمًا بِجَهَالَةٍ فَتُصْبِحُوا عَلَىٰ مَا فَعَلْتُمْ نَادِمِينَ﴾

📖 Al-Hujurat 6. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

jidar.x:
Hassan and Uncle Marzouq were neighbours in a narrow alley. Their front doors faced each other, and one single wall stood between their two houses.

They met every morning at their doors. They shook hands, each asked how the other was, and then each went off to his work. They were not very close, and they did not quarrel; and neither of them asked about things that were none of his business.

One night, Hassan got up from his sleep for something he needed, and he heard his neighbour's door opening quietly.

He climbed up to the roof and looked. He saw Uncle Marzouq going out in the dark, carrying a pot covered with a cloth. He closed the door behind him with both hands so it would not creak, and he walked on tiptoe as if he did not want anyone to hear him.

If Hassan had gone back to bed that night and forgotten about it, that would have been the end of the whole matter.

Hassan went back to bed, but he did not sleep.

He kept asking himself: What is Marzouq carrying in the pot? Where is he taking it? Why does he go out at night and not in the day? And every time he found an answer to one question, that answer gave him two more.

There was no sin in the questions themselves; a thought comes and goes. The sin is when a person gets up and follows it.

The next night, Hassan climbed onto the roof and waited — and the night after that too.

Every night Marzouq's door opened at the very same hour. He went out with his covered pot, and came back a while later with empty hands.

Uncle Marzouq became a long story in Hassan's head: with a beginning he had not seen, an ending he did not know, and a middle he had filled in with his own guesses.

On the fourth night, Hassan was not satisfied with just watching.

He came down from the roof and followed his neighbour, pressing himself against the walls, stopping when Marzouq stopped and walking when he walked.

As he walked, he told himself, "I only want to know. If there's something bad going on, I'll be the first to protect the alley from it."

And so he found himself a good-sounding excuse, and walked with it toward something he had no right to do.

Marzouq went from alley to alley until he reached the edge of the village, where the houses were smaller and poorer, and not a single door had a lamp.

Hassan followed him from far behind, counting his steps and making no sound, his heart pounding hard — as if he were the one doing something he was hiding from people.

And truly, he was the one doing that — not the man walking ahead of him.

Then Marzouq stopped at a low door with cracked wood.

He put the pot down on the doorstep and straightened the cloth over it so that the food would not get cold. Then he knocked once, softly, turned around, and hurried away before the door could open.

Every night he was carrying dinner to a house that had no dinner. And he went out in the dark so that the people of the house would not know who had fed them, and feel embarrassed.

Hassan saw all of this from behind the wall.

He was not happy with what he had found out, and he felt no relief. He just stood there with his hand on the cold mud wall, knowing something he had no right to know: a secret his neighbour had hidden from people because it was good, not because it was shameful.

Hassan wished he could give the secret back to its owner. But once a secret is taken, it cannot be given back.

In the morning, the two neighbours met at their doors as they did every morning.

Uncle Marzouq held out his hand, asked Hassan how he and his family were, and smiled as usual. He did not know that someone had followed him in the night, or that his secret was no longer a secret.

Hassan shook his hand and returned his salam, but he could not look him in the eye. That morning, Marzouq was the one of the two men with the lighter load.

The wall between the two houses stayed as it was, and Hassan never climbed onto the roof at night again.

﴿وَلَا تَجَسَّسُوا وَلَا يَغْتَب بَّعْضُكُم بَعْضًا﴾

There had never been anything bad behind the wall. Behind it was a man hiding his kindness from people — and a man who pulled away that cover when he had no right to.

📖 Al-Hujurat 12. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

kalima.x:
Sa'id was the village baker. Every day he woke up before dawn and lit the clay oven all by himself in the cold, so that when the market opened, his bread would be hot and waiting for people.

One morning the market opened as usual, and people passed by greeting one another. It was a day like any other; nothing big happened — except for one word that a man said and then walked away.

A man came to buy bread and found that the edge of one loaf was a little burnt.

He raised his voice and said a lot of things to Sa'id — far more than a slightly burnt loaf deserved — and he ended by saying, "I don't think you can do anything right!"

Then he took his bread and left, and he forgot what he had said before he reached the end of the market. But Sa'id did not forget a single word of it.

Sa'id stood silently with the loaf in his hand, looking down the road where the man had gone.

It was not the bread that hurt him; a burnt edge can be cut off and thrown away. What hurt was that the words were said in front of people, and that he had woken before dawn and lit the oven by himself, and no one had seen it.

The words stayed heavy in his chest, and he did not know where to put them down.

A little later Majid came with the sack of flour. Majid was a boy who brought flour to Sa'id every morning. That day he was a little late, and some of the flour spilled on the doorstep.

Sa'id spoke harshly to him, in a way he had never spoken to him before, full of a bad mood that was not Majid's fault at all.

Sa'id was not an unfair man. But he had been carrying heavy words since morning, and he put them down on the nearest shoulder.

Majid left the market with something in his chest that had not been there when he came in.

He passed his little brother and snapped at him. A neighbour asked him something, and he answered with half a word. He went into his house and did not say salam to anyone.

And so the word walked through the alleys from heart to heart. Each person thought he was the one who had been wronged, and no one knew that it all began with a loaf with a burnt edge.

The day dragged on heavily for the people of the village, and they did not know why it felt so heavy.

Here a short answer, there a door slammed shut; a salam not returned, a face turning away from another face. There was no real quarrel between them, nothing you could point to — but the bad mood was walking between the houses and catching everyone who passed.

All of it from one single word — and the man who said it was at home, not even remembering it.

At the well, Uncle Nassar was slowly filling his waterskin. Majid passed by with his face to the ground, not seeing anyone.

Uncle Nassar handed him the bucket and said, "How strong you are to carry that load, Majid! Your father must be proud of you."

Just a few words, no more. Uncle Nassar said them without waiting for any thanks, and went back to his waterskin.

Majid raised his head.

He did not say anything. It was only a few kind words from Uncle Nassar. But he felt something heavy leave his chest, and something light take its place, as if someone had lifted a load off his shoulder.

He walked on, and his walk was different from a moment before. He did not yet know where his feet would take him.

Then Majid went back to the market, though he had not planned to.

He said to Sa'id the baker, "Uncle, I picked up all the flour that spilled. And your bread today is even better than yesterday."

Sa'id looked at him for a long time without answering. Then he put his hand on Majid's shoulder and left it there for a moment. And the kind word walked through the alleys, just as the first word had.

In the morning the market opened as it did every morning. The bread came out hot from Sa'id's oven, and people greeted one another.

﴿وَقُولُوا لِلنَّاسِ حُسْنًا﴾

Nothing in the village had changed except two words: a harsh word that was said, and a kind word that undid it.

📖 Al-Baqarah 83. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

jabal.x:
Mazin was the tallest boy in the village, and the first of them to buy a new robe with money he had earned himself.

On the morning he bought it, he put it on before the sun was up and waited for people to come out. Then he went out into the alley and walked along it — not to go anywhere, but to pass by people so they would see him.

There was nothing wrong with the new robe. What was wrong was the way he walked.

At the bend in the alley, Uncle Awad had stopped to rest, with a heavy bundle of firewood on his back and his hand against the wall.

Mazin hurried past him. He did not say salam to him, and he did not offer him a hand.

Mazin had nothing against Uncle Awad and did not want to hurt him. He was just busy with himself, so he did not even see him.

Then Mazin stopped at the water trough to look at his reflection in it.

He liked what he saw. He smiled and kept looking, until that day he saw himself as taller than he really was — bigger than the alley he walked in, and bigger than the people walking in it with him.

The bigger Mazin grew in his own eyes, the smaller everything around him became.

Then he left the village for the road that crossed the plain.

There was no one on the road to see him: no house and no passer-by. Still, Mazin did not change the way he walked. He walked just as he had in the alley, stamping the dust with his feet and holding his head high, as if he wanted someone to see him who was not there.

That way of walking had become his habit; he walked like that even when no one was watching.

He walked for an hour, then turned to look behind him.

The village where he had strutted so proudly that morning was now far away and small, like a handful of clay at the edge of the plain. No one could be seen there, and no sound came from it.

Mazin was amazed: there, in that tiny place, he had been walking an hour ago as if he were the biggest thing in the world!

Then Mazin turned to face forward, and he saw what he had not been looking at.

He saw a huge mountain that filled the horizon from end to end, its peak disappearing into the clouds. The mountain had been in front of him ever since he left the village, but he had not seen it, because the whole way he had been looking at his robe.

So he walked toward it, not taking his eyes off it.

Mazin walked for an hour or more until he reached the foot of the mountain, and he stood beneath it, tired from walking.

He put his palm on the rock and found it cold and rough. It did not care about Mazin's robe or who he was.

Then he lifted his head to look at the peak, and he could not see where it ended. Here, beneath this great mountain, the tallest boy in the village was no longer tall.

No one said anything to him. No one laughed at him or mocked him; there was no one else in that place but him.

But he stood quietly under the rock, and he remembered Uncle Awad, whom he had passed without seeing. He remembered the way he had walked in the alley, and his face in the water trough.

His face turned red with shame — and there was no one there to see it.

Then Mazin went back along the same road, still in his robe, now a little dusty.

When he came into the alley, he saw Uncle Awad, who had put his bundle down on the ground to rest. Mazin went over to him, lifted the bundle onto his own shoulder, and carried it ahead of him to his house, without saying anything or waiting for thanks.

That day, people saw nothing special about the way he walked.

And the mountain stayed where it was, not knowing that a boy had come to it and gone back.

﴿وَلَا تَمْشِ فِي الْأَرْضِ مَرَحًا ۖ إِنَّكَ لَن تَخْرِقَ الْأَرْضَ وَلَن تَبْلُغَ الْجِبَالَ طُولًا﴾

There was no teacher or preacher on Mazin's road. There was only a great mountain, and a boy who lifted his head and looked at it.

📖 Al-Isra' 37. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

hajar.x:
In Suhail's village there was a stone water channel. It took water from a spring at the foot of the mountain and carried it past the houses until it poured it into a wide field.

Every house and every palm tree drank from this channel, and it watered the field that fed the whole village. None of them knew who had built it or when; they had simply found it there and benefited from it.

One winter night, part of the channel collapsed.

One stone fell and pulled two more down with it, leaving a gap in the channel wall as wide as two arms. The water poured out of it onto the soil, and the soil drank it up right there.

When morning came, not a single drop reached the field. The gap was not big, but it was right where all the water passed through.

In the morning, people came to look at the gap and stood at its edge.

One said, "This isn't next to my land." Another said, "Whoever broke it should fix it." A third said, "It needs ten men, and we're busy."

Then each of them went back home. None of them said anything untrue or unfair — but the water kept running away into the soil.

Only one boy stayed by the gap. His name was Suhail, and he did not say anything.

Suhail owned nothing in the field. He could not do what the men could do, and no one listened to his opinion.

But he looked at the water disappearing into the soil, and then at the green field at the end of the path, and he counted how many days it would stay green before it turned yellow.

Then Suhail climbed down into the channel and took hold of the nearest stone.

The stone was heavy for him. He dragged it through the mud bit by bit, until he propped it back in its place in the wall.

Then he sat down to catch his breath and looked at the gap. It was almost the same — only a tiny bit smaller.

So Suhail got up and went to the second stone.

People passed by him, going and coming. They saw him, and no one said anything to him. No one stopped him, and no one helped him.

The whole day went by like that: Suhail in the channel lifting a stone and setting it down, and the gap shrinking by only one hand-span all day long.

Suhail did not think he would fix the channel by himself. He was only starting.

On the morning of the second day, people came out and found Suhail in his place, as if he had never left it.

Uncle Jabir stood at the edge and watched him for a long time. Then he took off his sandals, climbed down into the channel, lifted the stone Suhail had been dragging since morning, and set it in its place.

Uncle Jabir did not say to anyone, "Come and help," and he did not blame anyone for sitting idle.

Then down came the man who had said, "This isn't next to my land."

Then the one who had said, "Whoever broke it should fix it." Then the man with the animals came with a rope and a donkey. The women brought water and bread and stood at the edge, and the boys stood in a line from the pile of stones to the gap, passing them along to one another.

No one called them, and no one gave a speech.

When the last stone was set in place, the water rose in the channel. It paused for a moment at the new wall, and then flowed on.

It ran over the new stones as if the channel had never broken, flowed on past the houses until it reached the field, and went in.

After that day, no one could tell which stone in the wall had been the first stone.

By the end of the day, the field was as green as before.

﴿وَتَعَاوَنُوا عَلَى الْبِرِّ وَالتَّقْوَىٰ﴾

No single man fixed the channel. It was begun by Suhail, who owned nothing in the field, and finished by people who had been passing by — and climbed down.

📖 Al-Ma'idah 2. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

tamra.x:
Hajj Mubarak had been selling dates in the village market for forty years, and his granddaughter Salma sat beside him, holding the bags for him.

In the shop across from his, Faris sold dates too. Faris was a lively young man with the loudest voice in the market, calling out about his dates from dawn.

Their dates came from the same palm trees, and their scales were made by the same craftsman.

Whenever Hajj Mubarak weighed dates for someone, he waited patiently until the two pans of the scale stopped moving and were level. He never rushed, even when the line was long.

When they were level, he took one date from the pile with his right hand, put it in the bag on top of the weight, and then handed it over.

Salma saw this on the first day, and then she saw it with every bag after that. Her grandfather did it without even looking at the customer, as if that date were part of the weight.

Faris, though, was fast. He sold to three people in the time Hajj Mubarak sold to one.

He poured the dates, raised the scale, and lowered it in a flash, with the tip of his finger on the edge of the pan, pressing it so lightly you could hardly see. Then he emptied the bag before the pans had settled.

So every bag he sold was missing two or three dates, and no one noticed. And he sold a little cheaper than Hajj Mubarak.

By the second week, people were leaving Hajj Mubarak's shop and going to Faris's.

Salma, counting the bags that had not been sold, said, "Grandpa, Faris gives less and you give more, and people have gone to him!"

Hajj Mubarak said, without lifting his head from the scale, "The other pan isn't mine, Salma."

Salma did not understand what he meant, and he did not add anything more.

A whole month went by like that.

At Faris's there were crowds and noise, and bags being filled without stopping. At Hajj Mubarak's there were only one or two customers all morning, while Salma shooed flies off the dates with a palm frond.

Even so, Hajj Mubarak did not lower his price at all. He did not leave out the extra date for even one day, and he did not say a single word about Faris.

But bags are not opened in the market — they are opened at home.

Every day the mothers emptied the dates into the same dish, so they knew how much a pound of dates filled it, and how high it came.

Each of them noticed that her dish was coming up a little short, then a little shorter. No woman said anything to her neighbour, but each one understood.

Then people began coming back to Hajj Mubarak.

They did not all come back at once, and no one came to complain or shout. But one woman began sending her son to Hajj Mubarak's shop instead of Faris's, and then a man started walking past Faris without stopping.

Faris stood behind his pile of dates looking at the market, not knowing what had changed. The dates were the same dates, and his price was cheaper!

One morning, Faris stood for a long time watching Hajj Mubarak's hand: the pans settling, then the date, then the bag.

And Faris understood what he had not understood before. He went back to his scale, lifted his finger off the pan, and waited.

He waited until the pans were still, and the waiting was longer than he had thought. Then he took a date with his right hand and put it in the bag, and he did not look around to see if anyone had noticed.

Neither Hajj Mubarak nor Faris ever spoke about it.

But at the end of the day, Salma began to see something she had never seen before: a bag leaving Faris's shop with one date on top of the weight.

She looked at her grandfather, and he was smiling at his scale, as if the scale had done it. He did not say anything to her, and this time she did not ask.

Years later, when Salma had grown up, she understood what her grandfather had meant: every scale has one pan for you and one pan for someone else, and your hand should only ever hold your own pan.

﴿وَلَا تَبْخَسُوا النَّاسَ أَشْيَاءَهُمْ﴾

The extra date was not a generous gift for people to praise Hajj Mubarak for. It was there so that the other pan would never, ever come up short.

📖 Hud 85. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

fasila.x:
Amir and Nabil had a father who was a poor farmer. When he died, he left them nothing but a small piece of land at the edge of the oasis, where the palm trees end and the sand begins.

In his last days, he had planted two little palm shoots there with his own hands: one shoot for each son, each as long as an arm, with a low mud wall between them and a single well behind them.

The two brothers stood between the shoots, each looking at his share.

Amir looked at his shoot for a long time and said, "This won't feed anyone. It needs years before it gives dates, and I need food today."

What Amir said was not false, but he wanted something bigger than what he had in his hand, so all he could see in the shoot was how small it was.

When a caravan passed through the oasis, Amir packed his things and left with it, leaving his shoot to the sun and the wind.

Nabil, though, sat down by his shoot, brushed the sand off its leaves with his palm, and said, "Alhamdulillah. It's small, but it's mine, and my father planted it with his own hand."

Then he went to the well, filled the bucket, and watered it. He watered it the next day, and the day after that. And each time he said the same words, as if he were saying them for the first time.

Nabil's thankfulness was not just words on his tongue.

He got up before the heat grew strong and watered his shoot. Then he piled soil around it into a little basin to hold the water, and tied its young fronds to a stick so the wind would not break them.

He knew that a palm shoot needs only water and patience. So he gave it water and patience, and he did not hurry it to grow.

Then summer came, and with it came a hot wind carrying sand.

Nabil built a fence of dry palm fronds around his shoot to keep the wind off it. And whenever there was water left in his bucket, he watered his brother Amir's shoot with it.

But one bucket is not enough for two plots of land. Amir's shoot bent in the wind, its fronds turned yellow and dried up, while its owner was far away with the caravan.

The years went by.

Nabil's shoot became a great palm tree, taller than two men, with a thick trunk and fronds that shaded the well.

On the other side of the wall, in Amir's land, there was nothing left but a short dry stump, showing that something had once been there and then died.

The land was the same land, the well was the same well, and the two shoots had once been exactly one arm long.

One summer, the first cluster of golden fresh dates appeared on the palm tree.

Nabil climbed up to it slowly and cut it. Then he came down, sat in the palm's shade, and ate the first date with his right hand. It was sweeter than he had imagined.

Then he lifted his head to the fronds and said the same words he used to say when his shoot was only as long as his arm: "Alhamdulillah."

And the palm tree did not stop with itself.

Little shoots grew out from its base. Nabil pulled them out gently so as not to hurt the mother tree, planted them around it, and watered them just as he had watered their mother.

One palm became five, then five became ten, until Nabil's land was full of palm trees. And all of it came from one little shoot as long as an arm.

After many long years, Amir came back from his travels, tired, with very little left in his hands.

He stood at the wall looking at his brother's palm trees, then at the dry stump in his own land, and he said nothing. Nabil said nothing to him either.

Then Nabil pulled out a shoot from the base of the first palm tree, handed it to him with both hands, and said, "This is from our father's palm tree, Amir. Start with this."

Amir planted it in his land, in the very spot where his first shoot had died, and carried water to it on its very first morning.

﴿لَئِن شَكَرْتُمْ لَأَزِيدَنَّكُمْ﴾

Nabil's thankfulness was not a word he said once — it was water he carried every morning. And Allah gave him more: from one little shoot, a land full of palm trees.

📖 Ibrahim 7. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

siyaj.x:
Uncle Sultan and his neighbour Mar'i lived in two stone houses side by side, on a terrace on the mountainside.

Uncle Sultan had a small garden of onions and broad beans, surrounded by a fence of thorny branches. Mar'i had three goats in a pen whose gate did not close properly.

Between the garden and the pen there were only two steps.

One morning Uncle Sultan went out to his garden and found the fence broken, with the three goats in the middle of it eating his beans and trampling whatever they had not eaten.

He looked up, and there was Mar'i on his rooftop, looking at him.

Mar'i said, "They're goats — they don't know about boundaries!" and went back inside. He did not mean any harm; he just did not think it was his problem.

Uncle Sultan did not shout. He did not hit the goats, and he did not bang on his neighbour's door.

Instead, he gently gathered them with his stick, led them back to their pen, closed the gate on them, and tied it with a rope of his own.

Then he went back to his garden, where half the season's crop was lost. He gathered what was left of the beans and sat down to mend the fence, as if the wind had broken it.

But it happened again.

Once a week, then twice. And every time, Uncle Sultan led the goats back to their pen, tied the gate, and went back to mend his fence, branch by branch.

People passing by would tell him, "Complain about Mar'i to everyone!" And Uncle Sultan would say, "He's my neighbour," and carry on with his work.

One day Mar'i travelled to the city for something he needed, and left the goats in their pen.

That night the first snow fell. The pen had no roof, so the goats stood in it shivering with cold, with no shelter and no one to open the gate for them.

Uncle Sultan heard them bleating from behind the wall. He took his lamp and went out to them.

He gathered them one by one, brought them into his own house's animal shed, and closed the door behind them.

Then he brushed the snow off them with his hand, spread out some of his straw for them, and put in front of them some of the feed he had been saving for winter.

He sat with them for a while in the lamplight until they stopped shivering. Then he put out the lamp and went to sleep, his clothes still wet with snow.

Mar'i came back in the morning, with snow up to his knees on the road.

He found his pen's gate open — and nothing inside! He stood in the snow not knowing where to look. There were no tracks around the pen; the snow had covered every trace.

He was afraid a wolf had got to them before him. Then he heard bleating nearby… coming from his neighbour's shed.

Mar'i walked through the snow to Uncle Sultan's house and knocked on the door, not knowing what he would say.

Uncle Sultan opened the shed for him, and there were the three goats on the straw, warm and full, as if the night had never happened.

Uncle Sultan did not say anything about the fence, or the beans, or all the many times he had stopped counting.

Mar'i looked at him for a long time, then said in a low voice, "I thought you hated me, Uncle Sultan. I thought every fence you mended was a way of blaming me."

Uncle Sultan said, "I have never hated you, Mar'i. You're my neighbour, and a neighbour isn't answered with a fence."

Mar'i lowered his head, and he felt something in his chest melt away, just as the snow was melting off his shoulders.

In the spring, people saw Uncle Sultan and Mar'i building a stone wall together between the garden and the pen: Mar'i lifting the stones, and Uncle Sultan setting each one in its place.

﴿ادْفَعْ بِالَّتِي هِيَ أَحْسَنُ فَإِذَا الَّذِي بَيْنَكَ وَبَيْنَهُ عَدَاوَةٌ كَأَنَّهُ وَلِيٌّ حَمِيمٌ﴾

The wall was not there to separate the two neighbours, but to protect what was between them.

📖 Fussilat 34. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

fakhkhar.x:
Uncle Mansour was a potter. He had a small workshop at the entrance to the village, on the road where the caravans passed. He had worked there since he was a young man, until the clay obeyed him.

In the spring, Ziyad came to learn the craft. Ziyad was clever and quick with his hands, but he rushed everything, and whenever a jar leaned over in his hands, he got angry.

Uncle Mansour would laugh and tell him, "Ziyad, clay doesn't obey a hurried hand."

One day Ziyad sat down at the potter's wheel for the tenth time — that's the wheel that spins the clay until it becomes a jar — and the jar leaned in his hands and collapsed.

He slapped the clay angrily with his palm, then looked at Uncle Mansour, waiting to be scolded.

But Uncle Mansour said nothing. He put down what he was doing, came and sat behind Ziyad, placed his hands over Ziyad's hands on the clay, and turned the wheel with him slowly.

At noon, a poor stranger stopped at the door of the workshop, worn out by the long road and by hunger.

He said in a low voice, "Do you have some water, or a piece of bread?"

Ziyad lifted his head from the clay and said sharply, "Go away, we're working!" and waved him off. The man left without a word and did not look back.

The wheel stopped, and the whole workshop went quiet, so quiet you could hear the wind on the road.

Uncle Mansour had taken his foot off the wheel. He sat looking at Ziyad, the clay drying on his hands.

There was no anger on his face, but his look made Ziyad lower his eyes to the ground and wish he could take his words back.

Then Uncle Mansour got up, washed his hands, took a small jar of water and two loaves from their lunch, and went out.

He walked down the road after the stranger, slowly as always, until he caught up with him at the lote tree at the edge of the village.

Ziyad stayed standing at the door, watching them from far away, not knowing whether to follow or stay where he was.

Uncle Mansour sat with the man in the shade of the lote tree and handed him the water with his right hand, and then the bread.

He did not ask him where he had come from, or why he was asking people for help. He just sat with him while he ate and drank, and they talked a little about the road and the rain, the way two men talk when they meet.

Then the man stood up, made du'a for him, and went on his way, his back a little straighter.

Uncle Mansour came back to the workshop, and Ziyad said, without lifting his eyes, "We only have a little, Uncle."

Uncle Mansour said, "I didn't give to him because we have a lot, Ziyad. Someone who stands at the door and asks has already had something break inside him before he could ask. So don't you break what is left."

Then he went back to his wheel and said nothing more.

A few days later, Uncle Mansour went to the market, and Ziyad stayed alone in the workshop.

An old woman leaning on a stick stopped at the door, asking for something to eat.

All Ziyad had was half a loaf — his own lunch. He looked at it, then at the woman. Then he got up and went to her himself, and handed her the bread with his right hand, along with a cup of water.

The woman made a long du'a for him. Ziyad felt shy and said, "It's all I have today, Auntie. If I had more, I'd give it to you."

His voice was gentle — a voice he had never heard from himself before.

When the woman had gone, he went back to the wheel and found his hands calmer than before, and the clay turned between them without leaning.

In the evening Uncle Mansour came back and found on the shelf a straight jar that did not lean at all, made by Ziyad all by himself.

﴿وَأَمَّا السَّائِلَ فَلَا تَنْهَرْ﴾

Afterwards, Ziyad never knew which of the two had taught him patience: the clay between his hands, or the stranger who had stood at the door.

📖 Ad-Duha 10. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

ghina.x:
At the edge of the village there was a small kuttab — a place where little children learn the Quran. Every morning the girls sat there on a straw mat, reciting in front of their teacher, Umm Salim.

Dima was always the first to arrive. She left her house before the sun rose and walked down the road alone, with nothing in her hand but her writing board.

Dima's house was one of the smallest in the village, and her father worked on other people's land.

When the morning grew late, the teacher let the girls rest, and each one took out what she had brought: one had bread and olives, another a handful of dates.

Hana sat next to Dima. She would untie her little cloth bundle and eat, chatting and laughing.

But Dima took nothing out, because she had nothing with her. She would put her board on her knees and look at it, as if she were going over what she had memorised.

Dima could smell the bread, and her tummy would rumble. She looked at the dates in Hana's hand and wished she could have one.

The words were so close: "Give me one." Just three words. If she had said them, she would have been given some, for these were her friends, and none of them was stingy.

But every time the words reached the tip of her tongue, she pressed her lips shut over them and turned her face toward the door.

Whenever she left home, her mother would tell her, "Dima, don't hold out your hand to anyone. What we have at home is enough for us, even if it's little."

When the hunger got hard, she went to the big water jar by the door and drank until she was full. Then she wiped her mouth and went back to her place on the mat.

She never told anyone she was hungry, and she never asked Hana for a single date.

Then the lesson ended, and the girls went out laughing. Dima and Hana walked down the road with the sun above their heads.

Hana said, "Dima, where's your food? I've never seen you eat with us."

Dima said, "I eat at home." And that was true: her mother baked them a loaf in the evening that was enough, and sat with them until they had finished.

Days went by like this: Dima left before sunrise, sat on the mat, and recited, and when it was time to eat, she drank from the water jar and stayed quiet.

She memorised faster than all the other girls, until Umm Salim began asking her to recite alone, with the others repeating after her.

In all those days she never asked anyone for anything, and no one knew she was hungry.

One day at the end of summer, her hunger was so strong that her voice grew weak as she recited. The teacher let her stop and did not ask her about it in front of the girls.

Dima went out into the kuttab's courtyard and sat alone in the shade of the wall, while the girls ate by the door.

She closed her eyes for a moment, then opened them, and she did not go to anyone.

The next day, Hana came with a bundle bigger than usual. She untied it, and inside were two loaves.

She handed one to Dima with her right hand and said, "My mum baked lots today, and I can't eat two loaves."

Dima looked at her quietly, then took the loaf and said, "Jazakillahu khayran — may Allah reward you with good." And they ate together in the shade of the tamarisk tree.

Then a new girl came to the kuttab, from a house at the far end of the village. She sat in the last row and took nothing out when the other girls did.

Dima knew what was wrong. She got up and went to her without asking her anything, broke her loaf in two, and handed her half with her right hand.

The girl took it, looking at the ground, and then raised her eyes to Dima.

Umm Salim saw this, and after the lesson she said to her, "Dima, you never asked anyone, and people gave to you — and then you became the one who gives. Today you are the richest girl in this kuttab."

The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever seeks to be free of need from people, Allah will make him rich."

And Dima walked home the way she did every day — happy and at peace, with her head held high and a generous heart.

📖 Narrated by Al-Bukhari. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

ruqayya.x:
Ruqayya's house was at the edge of the village. It had a courtyard with a clay oven and a single palm tree.

Her mother baked bread there every evening. She worked alone from late afternoon until sunset and hardly ever sat down.

Ruqayya was twelve years old, and she loved embroidery. She would sit with it wherever the light was, and once she held the needle, she barely heard anything around her.

One evening Ruqayya sat by the door, embroidering a dress she had started days before, and the thread was moving in her hand just the way she liked.

Her mother called her from the courtyard: "Ruqayya, come and help me with the dough."

She said, "In a minute." And she did not get up. Her mother called a second time, and then a third, and each time she said, "In a minute," without lifting her eyes from the thread.

Then Ruqayya threw the dress down and got up, saying loudly, "Uff! It's always me, every day! Isn't there anyone else in this house?"

Her mother went quiet and did not answer her with a single word. She gave her one look, then went back to her dough.

That look was heavier on Ruqayya than any scolding. If her mother had shouted at her, it would have been easier.

Ruqayya went into her room, shut the door behind her, and sat waiting for the anger in her chest to calm down.

Her mother stayed alone in the courtyard: kneading, lighting the oven, and taking out the bread, as night fell around her.

The house was silent that night. There was only the sound of the fire, and the sound of the loaves being placed on the tray, one after another.

Then her little sister Bushra came in, sat down beside her, and said, "Ruqayya, why is Mama so quiet? Are you upset with her?"

Ruqayya could not find an answer to give her. She said, "Go to sleep, Bushra."

Bushra fell asleep holding the edge of Ruqayya's dress, and Ruqayya lay looking at the ceiling, the words she had said going round and round in her head.

Ruqayya remembered the time she was sick when she was little, when she had a high fever for three nights and could not get out of bed.

Her mother sat by her head, putting cool water on her forehead and reciting Quran over her, and she did not sleep until Ruqayya slept.

Then when morning came, she got up and went to work as if she had slept all night, and she never told anyone she was tired.

Ruqayya did not sleep that night. She tossed and turned until, late in the night, she heard her mother get up, make wudu, and pray.

Then she heard her making du'a in sujud — and she heard her own name in that du'a.

Ruqayya put her hand over her mouth so no one would hear her. Her eyes filled with tears in the dark, and she said to herself, "And I'm the one who said those things to her."

When it was a little before Fajr, Ruqayya got up in the dark, put on her clothes, and went out to the courtyard.

She kneaded the rest of the flour the way she had seen her mother do it, lit the oven, and baked until the tray was full.

Her hands were shaking from the cold and from too little sleep, but she was smiling, and watching the door to see when it would open.

When her mother came out at Fajr, she found the oven burning, the bread laid out, and Ruqayya standing there waiting for her.

Ruqayya walked to her, took her hand and kissed it, then kissed her head and said, "Forgive me, Mama."

Her mother did not say anything, but she held her close for a long time. Then they sat and baked together until the sun came up.

From that day on, whenever Ruqayya felt upset, she stayed quiet until the feeling passed, and only then did she speak.

﴿فَلَا تَقُل لَّهُمَا أُفٍّ وَلَا تَنْهَرْهُمَا وَقُل لَّهُمَا قَوْلًا كَرِيمًا﴾

And she would tell Bushra, "A word that leaves your mouth never comes back, so be careful where you put it."

📖 Al-Isra' 23. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

shatla.x:
In the courtyard of their house, Badr had a row of ten seedlings that he had planted with his own hands. He watered them every morning before the sun grew hot.

Every day he counted them one by one, picked the pebbles off them, and waited for them to grow.

Badr got angry quickly, and he knew it. Whenever someone told him off, he would say, "That's just how I was made. I can't help being angry."

One morning his friend Thamir came to help him. He picked up the bucket and walked along the row.

His foot tripped on a stone he had not seen. The bucket fell from his hand, and all the water spilled over two seedlings, which flopped over into the mud.

Thamir stood there not knowing what to do, then said, "Forgive me, Badr! Wallahi, I didn't mean it — I didn't see the stone."

Badr looked at the two seedlings, and then at Thamir. Something like fire rose in his chest, and his ears filled with the pounding of his heart.

He knew this feeling, and he knew what came after it; he had felt it many times before. But he did not hold himself back. He did not sit down, and he did not keep quiet.

He shouted at Thamir so loudly that the neighbours heard, and he said things to him he would never have said if he had stayed quiet for just a little while.

Then Badr kicked the soil, and a third seedling went flying. He kicked again, and a whole row was torn out.

He did not stop until all ten seedlings lay scattered on the ground, with water running between them.

Then he stood looking at his hands and at the ground. A moment ago it had been two seedlings; now it was ten — and the one who had ruined the other eight was him, and no one else.

Thamir walked to the gate without turning around, and left without saying anything.

Badr sat on the ground among the torn-up seedlings, the water growing cold beneath him and the sun rising above him, with no one left in the courtyard.

What hurt him was that Thamir had ruined two without meaning to, while he had ruined eight, seeing exactly what he was doing — and no one had stopped him.

His grandfather Ayedh came and found him like that. He did not scold him or ask what had happened.

He sat down on the ground beside him, took a seedling from the mud, straightened its root, and planted it again. Then he handed Badr a seedling and said:

"Badr, anger is a guest. If you make it sit down with you, it will get up and leave. But if you walk along with it, it will take you somewhere you don't like — and then leave you there."

Together they replanted the rest of the seedlings until the row was straight again, and days went by. The seedlings put out leaves slowly, as every seedling does after being pulled up and planted back.

Badr watered them alone every morning, and Thamir no longer stopped by as he used to.

Every time he looked at the row, he remembered his own hand, not his friend's, and it made him feel bad — but he did not know how to start talking to him.

Then one goat slipped in through the courtyard gate when he was not looking, bit the top off one seedling in the row, and ran away before he could reach it.

The very same thing rose in his chest, his ears filled with the pounding of his heart, and he was about to shout.

But he remembered his grandfather's words. He sat down on the ground right where he was, closed his mouth, shut his eyes, and counted silently until the feeling went away.

When the anger had left him, he got up, straightened what was left of the nibbled seedling, watered it, and broke nothing.

Then he took one seedling from his row and walked with it down the road to Thamir's house, and found him standing at the door.

He handed him the seedling with his right hand and said, "This is for you to plant at your house. I'm the one who ruined my row with my own hand — not you."

Weeks went by, and the row grew straight and green, and Thamir came every morning carrying the bucket.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do not get angry."

And Badr would tell the people he knew, "I used to say, 'That's how I am, I can't help it.' But the way to help it was to sit down."

📖 Narrated by Al-Bukhari. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

salam.x:
Mish'al and Talal were neighbours. The door of one house faced the door of the other, and the well sat between them in the middle of the square.

Every morning they went out together to fill water for both houses, then sat on the edge of the well talking until the sun grew hot.

Whenever the people of the village saw one of them alone, they would ask, "Where's your friend?" And he would laugh and say, "Right behind me — he's coming."

One morning, as they were pulling up the bucket together, the rope slipped from their hands, and the bucket fell into the well. They heard it land far below.

Mish'al said, "You let go of it!"

Talal said, "No, you did! I was holding my side."

The bucket belonged to Talal's house. It was new — his father had bought it at the market the week before.

Their voices grew louder until the people in the houses could hear them, and each said things to the other that he had never said before.

Then Talal said one word that hurt Mish'al more than the bucket did, and Mish'al answered him with one just like it.

Then they fell silent, each waiting for the other to apologise. That silence was heavier on them than all the words.

Then each of them turned and walked to his own door, without saying anything to the other or looking back.

Mish'al went in and shut his door, and Talal went in and shut his. The square stayed empty between them, with the rope swinging over the mouth of the well.

It was the first day they had been apart since they had known each other, and neither of them thought it would last long.

The next day, Mish'al went out alone to the well before everyone else, lowered his rope, filled water for his house, and went back.

Talal came out after him and found the rope wet, so he knew his friend had been there first. He filled his water and went back.

The second day passed without a single word between them. Each of them came to know when the other went out, and waited until later so as not to meet him at the well.

On the third day, Talal stood behind his door. When he heard the sound of the bucket, he knew Mish'al was in the square.

He would put his hand on the door, then take it away, saying to himself, "He's the one who started it, so he's the one who should come back."

And at that very moment Mish'al was standing at the well, saying the very same thing to himself, not knowing that his friend was behind the door.

On the evening of the third day, his grandmother Noura passed by and saw him at the door looking out at the square. She sat down beside him and said:

"Talal, three days have gone by. The fourth day is not like the third, and the fifth is not like the fourth — until the heart forgets how things used to be."

Then she got up, leaning on her stick, and went inside, leaving him at the door to think.

Talal could not sleep until very late that night. He counted all the years between him and Mish'al, and then counted the words that had passed between them in one single hour.

He said to himself, "Even if he was the one who said the first word, I don't have to wait for him."

Late in the night he fell asleep, knowing what he would do when dawn came — and he told no one.

At dawn, Talal went out earlier than usual and found Mish'al at the well, twisting the rope.

He walked up to him, stood in front of him, held out his right hand, and said, "As-salamu alaykum, Mish'al."

Mish'al raised his head and was silent for a moment, not knowing what to say. Then he took his hand with his right hand and said, "Wa alaykum as-salam." And there were tears in his eyes.

Then they tied a long rope together and let it down, and kept searching the bottom of the well until the bucket caught on it. They pulled it out, and they laughed.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "It is not allowed for a Muslim to stay away from his brother for more than three days… and the better of the two is the one who greets first with salam."

Afterwards Talal would say, "I lost nothing by going first — and I thought I would lose."

📖 Agreed upon (Al-Bukhari and Muslim). This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

ukhtan.x:
Reem and Hessa were sisters, four years apart. Every morning they carried the water jar from the well to the house together.

Reem took the right handle and Hessa took the left, and they walked slowly so the water would not spill.

On the way they would argue about little things, and then forget all about it before they got home.

One morning Hessa fell a step behind. The jar tipped, and water spilled all over Reem's dress, soaking it.

Reem put the jar down and said, "You're little and you can't do it right. Walk by yourself — I'll carry it alone."

Hessa said, "I can do it right! You're the one who went too fast!" But Reem did not listen to her. She lifted the jar by herself and walked off.

Hessa stood still on the road, watching her sister's back as she walked away, until she was far ahead.

She did not cry. But she walked behind her at a distance, putting her feet where Reem had put hers, and she did not come closer.

She told herself, "One day I'll be big, and I'll carry the jar all by myself from the well to the house. Then she'll see."

Reem walked on with the jar alone. Before she had gone ten steps, it grew heavy. She kept moving it from one hand to the other, and then hugged it to her chest.

It was their mother's jar — one of the big ones that can only be carried with two hands.
