Reem knew all that. But she did not look behind her or call her sister, and she refused to put the jar down.

Then her foot went into a little hole in the road. She stumbled, the jar slipped out of her hands, and it fell onto a stone.

It broke. The water ran into the dust, and Reem sat among the broken pieces without saying a word.

The house was so close she could almost see its door, but at that moment it seemed very, very far away.

Hessa came running from behind and sat down next to her. She did not say, "I told you so."

Instead, she reached out and picked up a piece of the broken jar, then another, then another, gathering them one by one in the lap of her dress.

Reem looked at her for a long time. Then she reached out and gathered pieces with her, and they did not speak until they had picked up every last piece from the road.

Their father was building the courtyard wall. He saw them come in with the broken pieces, and he did not scold either of them.

He took one stone and stood it up alone; it wobbled and fell. Then he stood two stones together, each one holding up the other, and they stayed firm.

Then he said, "That's how sisters are, my girls. One stone alone falls, even if it's the biggest stone. But when they hold each other up, the wall stands."

The next day their mother brought out another jar from the house, gave it to them, and said, "This is the last one we have, so take good care of it."

Reem took the right handle, then looked at her sister and held out her other hand to her.

Hessa took hold of the left handle, and they walked slowly, just as they used to, and not a drop of water spilled.

One day three girls from the village were standing by the well. When the two sisters came, the girls looked at Hessa's patched dress and laughed.

Hessa felt ashamed and looked at the ground.

Reem stepped forward and stood right beside her, took her right hand, looked at the girls, and said, "This is my sister." Then the two of them walked off together and did not look back.

Days and days went by. Hessa grew bigger, and the road from the well to the house became shorter than it used to be.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "A believer to another believer is like a building — each part holds up the other."

And whenever Reem was asked about the first jar, she would say, "I broke it the day I carried it alone."

📖 Agreed upon (Al-Bukhari and Muslim). This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

hilal.x:
Hilal was eleven years old. He spoke slowly, and sometimes a word got stuck in his mouth, so he would repeat it once or twice until it came out.

Every night he climbed up to the roof of the house with his grandfather Abdullah. They sat on the straw mat and looked at the sky until they grew sleepy.

In the afternoons, the boys of the neighbourhood played in the square: Fahd, Bandar, and Adel. When Hilal came to talk to them, Fahd would repeat his words, stumbling just like him, and the others would laugh.

Then they called him "Father of the Stars," because he walked with his head up toward the sky.

Sometimes Hilal laughed along with them. Then he would go home and not say a word until dinner.

That night, when he climbed up to the roof, his grandfather pointed to a small, still star and said, "That is Al-Jadi, the North Star. All the stars move around, and it alone never leaves its place."

Then he said, "Our village is in its direction from the desert. Anyone who is lost at night and sees it will know his way."

Hilal repeated it slowly until he had learned it by heart.

The rain came at the end of winter, and Fahd said, "Tomorrow let's go out into the desert to gather desert truffles."

Hilal said, "I'll come with you." Fahd laughed and said, "You walk slowly and you talk slowly — when will we ever get back?"

When Grandfather Abdullah heard about it, he told them, "Take him with you. He won't slow you down." So they took him, though they did not want to.

They set out after noon and walked among the sand dunes, digging wherever the ground was cracked. They found lots of truffles — a kind of food like little potatoes that hides under the sand after the rain. They filled their bags and were very happy.

When the sun began to sink, Hilal said slowly, "The sun… is setting. Let's go back."

Fahd copied him as usual, they laughed, and they went on digging.

Then the sun set the way it sets in the desert, and a wind blew and wiped their footprints off the sand.

They stood among dunes that all looked the same. Bandar said, "We came from here." Adel said, "No, from over there." Fahd did not know anything, so he kept quiet.

The boys became very, very scared.

Hilal had lifted his head to the sky, as he did every night. He searched until he found the small, still star.

He said slowly, "That's… Al-Jadi. Our village… is that way."

The boys looked at one another. Then Fahd said in a quiet voice, "Walk in front of us, Hilal."

So Hilal walked in front, and they walked behind him in a line, none of them saying a word.

The words stumbled in his mouth, but his feet did not stumble on the way. Every time they climbed a dune, he lifted his head to the star and then went on.

After a long time in the night, the lights of the village appeared.

Their families had come out with lanterns to the edge of the village, and Grandfather Abdullah was among them.

The boys ran to them, and before his father could ask him anything, Fahd said, "Hilal is the one who brought us back."

Hilal said nothing. He put his bag of truffles in front of his grandfather.

The next night, four boys climbed up to Grandfather Abdullah's roof, not just one. They sat on the mat and looked at the sky.

Hilal showed them the stars, speaking slowly, and no one copied him.

﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا لَا يَسْخَرْ قَوْمٌ مِّن قَوْمٍ عَسَىٰ أَن يَكُونُوا خَيْرًا مِّنْهُمْ﴾

📖 Al-Hujurat 11. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

sahrij.x:
In the middle of the village there was a big stone cistern. It filled up with the winter rain, and the people of the village drank from it until the rain came back.

Uncle Abu Khalil looked after it. Every morning he filled two jars for each house — never giving one house more than another.

Lina came for her family's two jars with her little brother Karam. When she got home, she would pour some of the water over the courtyard to cool it, splash Karam so he laughed, and wash her doll's clothes twice every day.

Her mother told her, "Lina, this is the whole village's water, and there's a long summer between us and the rain."

Lina said, "The cistern is big, Mama. What difference does one jar make?"

Lina was not the only one who said that. In every house there was someone saying the same thing, and pouring out water just like she did.

Every evening Uncle Abu Khalil looked into the cistern, then walked away without saying anything.

Their neighbour, Auntie Umm Jamil, was an old woman who lived alone. When she made wudu, she collected the water in a bowl, and then watered the basil plant on her windowsill with it.

Lina watched her over the wall and wondered, saying to herself, "How careful she is with water!"

When summer grew hot, Uncle Abu Khalil let the bucket down into the cistern, and it did not reach the water until he had let out the whole rope.

He gathered the villagers and said, "From today, one jar for each house. If what's left is enough for us, we'll make it to the rain. If not, all we'll have is the faraway spring down in the valley."

Now one jar had to do for drinking, for kneading dough, and for wudu — everything. The heat grew stronger, and Karam got thirsty before the afternoon, and there was nothing left in the jar.

Lina went out to the courtyard and saw the ground where she had poured water for days, now dry and cracked. Not a trace of that water was left.

She sat by the door and cried. Auntie Umm Jamil saw her over the wall, called her over, and gave her a cup of water, saying, "This is what I have left from yesterday's jar."

Lina said, "But what about you, Auntie?" She said, "I know what summer is like, my dear. I only pour water where it does some good."

Lina gave her brother a drink, then went back to Auntie Umm Jamil and said, "Teach me."

From that day on, she covered the jar, drank from the small cup, and saved the leftover washing water to water the grapevine.

And whenever Karam splashed her, she said, "No, Karam — this is the village's water."

The summer days passed slowly and heavily. Every morning Uncle Abu Khalil filled the jars one by one, until there was only a little left at the bottom of the cistern.

Then one autumn morning the sky turned dark, and people heard thunder.

The villagers came out into the square. The rain poured into the cistern, and the children ran about under it.

Lina ran home, brought a big bowl, and put it where the rainwater came pouring off the roof. And Auntie Umm Jamil brought her bowl and put it right beside it.

﴿وَكُلُوا وَاشْرَبُوا وَلَا تُسْرِفُوا ۚ إِنَّهُ لَا يُحِبُّ الْمُسْرِفِينَ﴾

📖 Al-A'raf 31. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

sibaq.x:
Every spring the village held a race. The boys ran from the school yard to the big oak tree at the top of the hill.

Samer was the fastest of them every year. But this spring he twisted his foot a few days before the race, so he sat at home, sad, counting the days.

Then Mr Nabih, the teacher, came to see him and said, "You won't run this year, Samer, but I want you to be the judge. You'll stand by the oak tree and tell us who touches it first."

Samer was happy — then he went quiet. He knew that the fastest boys after him were two: his friend Wassim, and Ghassan.

In the winter, Ghassan had laughed at him in front of the boys when his foot slipped in the mud, and he had never said a word of sorry afterwards.

As for Wassim, he came to him every evening and said, laughing, "You're the judge this year, so Ghassan won't beat me!"

When race day came, Samer stood by the oak tree, leaning on his stick, and the people of the village gathered on both sides of the path.

Then Mr Nabih raised his hand in the school yard, and the boys set off, running up the hill.

As they came close to the oak tree, only two were left at the front: Wassim and Ghassan, shoulder to shoulder, with people shouting their names.

Then they both reached out their hands at the same moment and touched the trunk of the oak tree — with a tiny difference between them that no one saw except Samer.

Samer had seen Ghassan's palm touch the trunk before Wassim's.

Wassim turned to him, panting, his eyes saying, "Say my name." And Wassim's friends shouted, "Wassim! Wassim!"

Samer was silent for a moment, and he remembered the day of the mud.

Then he raised his hand and said in a loud voice, "Ghassan."

The people went quiet. Ghassan looked at him in surprise, as if he could not believe what he had heard.

And Wassim walked off down the hill without looking at his friend.

When Mr Nabih arrived, he asked Samer, "Did you see it with your own eyes?" He said, "Yes. He beat him by a finger's width."

So the teacher gave Ghassan the olive branch that is given to the winner. Ghassan took it, then came to Samer and said quietly, "Forgive me for the day of the mud."

In the evening Wassim knocked on Samer's door and sat beside him on the doorstep, silent for a long time.

Then he said, "I was angry with you. Then I thought: if you had said my name when I hadn't won, I would never have been happy with that olive branch, not for a single day."

From that year on, whenever the boys disagreed about something, they would say, "Let's ask Samer."

And Ghassan was the first to say it.

﴿وَلَا يَجْرِمَنَّكُمْ شَنَآنُ قَوْمٍ عَلَىٰ أَلَّا تَعْدِلُوا ۚ اعْدِلُوا هُوَ أَقْرَبُ لِلتَّقْوَىٰ﴾

📖 Al-Ma'idah 8. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

qindil.x:
On Uncle Abu Salim's door hung a lantern of copper and glass. He hung it up every evening, and it lit the whole alley right to the end.

The neighbourhood children played in its light after Maghrib, and Abu Salim never put it out until they had all gone home.

One evening Yazan was playing ball alone in the alley. He kicked it hard, and it flew up and hit the lantern. The glass shattered, and the light went out.

Yazan stood frozen in the dark. No one came out, and no one had seen him. So he grabbed his ball and hurried into his house.

In the morning Abu Salim stood at his door looking at the broken glass, and the neighbours gathered around him.

One of them said, "I saw Rami playing ball here yesterday." Rami was a boy whose family had just moved into the neighbourhood, and people did not know him yet.

Rami's mother came to apologise for her son, with Rami behind her saying, "I didn't do anything!" — but no one believed him.

Yazan was standing with the others, hearing and seeing everything. His heart was pounding, but his tongue would not move.

The day dragged on. Whenever Yazan saw Rami sitting alone on a stone at the edge of the neighbourhood, he looked at the ground and walked on.

When night came, he could not sleep. From his window he could see the alley lying dark — and he had never seen it dark before that night.

Early in the morning he got up, broke open his money box, gathered what was inside into a handkerchief, and walked to Abu Salim's house, his legs feeling heavy.

He knocked on the door, and Abu Salim came out. Yazan held out the handkerchief and said, "I broke the lantern, Uncle — not Rami."

Abu Salim looked at him for a long time. Then he gave the handkerchief back and said, "Glass for a lantern can be bought for a few coins, Yazan. But what you have brought me now can't be bought."

Then he said, "But there's one more thing you still need to do."

Abu Salim walked with him to Rami, and in front of him and the neighbours Yazan said, "I'm the one who broke it. I kept quiet while you got the blame."

Rami was quiet for a moment, then said, "I never thought anyone would clear my name." And he held out his hand to Yazan and shook it.

Then the three of them sat by the door. Abu Salim took out the broken glass and brought new glass, while Yazan and Rami held the lantern until he had fixed it in place.

He showed them how to wind the wire around the glass to hold it firm. Whenever the wire slipped from their fingers, he handed it back to them with a smile, until they got it right.

When evening came, Abu Salim hung the lantern on his door, and it lit the alley just as before.

The neighbourhood children played in its light — and Yazan and Rami played on the same team.

﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا اتَّقُوا اللَّهَ وَكُونُوا مَعَ الصَّادِقِينَ﴾

📖 At-Tawbah 119. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

tayyara.x:
Nizar and his cousin Fadi were never apart. They played in the olive grove behind the houses from morning until their families called them for lunch.

Nizar was the most skilful of all the boys with his hands. He made whistles out of reeds and little houses out of clay, and he did not think there was anything special about it.

One day Fadi's uncle came from the city and brought him a kite made of coloured paper — red, yellow, and green — with a long tail of ribbons.

When Fadi flew it on the hill, all the children of the village gathered around, shouting and pointing at it in the sky.

Nizar stood far away, watching it and not coming closer.

Fadi would call him, "Come on, Nizar, hold the string!" And he would say, "I don't want to." Then he went home and sat alone in the upstairs room.

He said to himself, "I wish it would tear."

On the third day, a strong wind blew and tugged at the kite. The string snapped out of Fadi's hand, and the kite flew off until it got caught at the top of an old olive tree, its paper torn on the branches.

Fadi stood under the tree and cried.

When Nizar saw it torn on the branch, he was not happy the way he had thought he would be.

Instead, he felt a tightness in his chest he had never felt before, and he went home with his head hanging down.

His grandmother, Umm Fawzi, saw him. She sat him down beside her and said, "What's the matter, Nizar?" He told her everything — even what he had said to himself.

She said, "My darling, you wished for it to be taken away from him; you didn't wish to have one like it. The One who gave Fadi a kite gave you two hands like no one else's in the whole village."

Nizar was quiet for a long time. Then he got up and climbed the olive tree — he was the best tree-climber of all the boys — and brought down the torn kite.

Then he went to the little river to cut reeds, and came back with paper, string, and glue made from flour. He sat in the upstairs room until Maghrib, not talking to anyone.

In the morning he knocked on Fadi's door with two kites in his hands.

The first was Fadi's very own kite: Nizar had bound up its broken sticks and patched its paper. The second was a brand-new kite of reeds and brown paper that he had made with his own hands.

They climbed the hill together and flew the two kites side by side: one colourful and patched, and one the colour of brown paper.

The village children gathered around them, and most of them were asking Nizar, "Will you make one for me?"

In those days Nizar would sit in the olive grove with the children around him, teaching them how to tie the reeds and glue the paper.

And Fadi held the string for him.

﴿وَلَا تَتَمَنَّوْا مَا فَضَّلَ اللَّهُ بِهِ بَعْضَكُمْ عَلَىٰ بَعْضٍ﴾

📖 An-Nisa' 32. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

kalb.x:
Every Thursday, Nour walked to her aunt Umm Firas's house in the next village, along a short dirt path between fig orchards, with a small water flask hanging from her shoulder.

One day in August, it was so hot that the dust stung her feet.

When she had gone halfway, she saw a thin dog by the dry water trough, stretched out in the shade of a rock, panting with its tongue on the dust.

By the trough were some boys from the village, Shadi among them. They were throwing pebbles at the dog and laughing, and the dog could not even get up.

When they saw Nour, Shadi said, "Stay away — that dog's got mange."

Nour was afraid of dogs. She stood far off and looked at the flask in her hand. There was only a little water in it, the path was still long, and the sun was right above her head.

Then she looked at the dog, and saw its eyes looking at her.

She told the boys, "Leave it alone." Then she came closer slowly. She found a small hollow in the rock, and poured all the water from her flask into it.

The dog crawled over to it and drank until there was nothing left, then lifted its head to look at her.

Shadi laughed and said, "You give water to a dog and walk on thirsty?" And the boys laughed with him.

Nour did not answer them. She went on her way, her throat dry with thirst.

When she reached her aunt's house, she was tired and her face was red. Her aunt gave her a drink and asked, "Where's the water from your flask?" So Nour told her.

Her aunt said, "Do you know, Nour, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ told of a man who gave water to a thirsty dog — and Allah thanked him for it and forgave him?"

Nour felt a joy she had never felt before, and she forgot how tired she was from the walk.

Then her aunt got up, filled the flask for her, gave her a small clay bowl, and said, "This is for the trough."

When Nour came back in the afternoon, she found that the dog had got up, and it came walking toward her, wagging its tail. She put the bowl by the trough and filled it.

Shadi was sitting on a rock nearby. This time he did not laugh. He got up, brought water from the little river, and poured it into the bowl.

From that day on, there was a bowl by the trough that never dried up; whoever passed by from the two villages would fill it. And every Thursday the dog walked with Nour all the way to her aunt's door, and then went back.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "There is a reward for kindness to every living creature."

📖 Agreed upon (Al-Bukhari and Muslim). This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

qafila.x:
Every autumn the village caravan set out for the city, carrying olive oil, raisins, and soap. It crossed a long desert to get there, travelling for days and nights.

Sheikh Abu Maher had led it for twenty years. He knew the way like the palm of his hand.

That year, Basil went with it for the first time. He was twelve years old, and he walked beside his father's camel, never tired of looking at the desert.

In the caravan was Uncle Arif, an old camel driver who did not talk much and who knew every single well in the desert.

On the third day, Abu Maher said, "We'll leave the old road and cut across here. It's a day shorter."

Uncle Arif said, "Abu Maher, there's little water that way, and there wasn't much rain this year." Abu Maher said, "I know," and went on without asking anyone else.

The caravan walked for two days through land none of them had ever crossed. When they reached the well Abu Maher had been aiming for, they found it dry, with nothing at the bottom but stones.

The waterskins had grown light, and the camels were groaning with thirst.

Abu Maher sat on a rock by the well in silence. People looked at him and said nothing.

Then he got up. That night he gathered the men of the caravan around the fire and said, "I made a mistake when I went by my own opinion alone. So tell me what you think — all of you."

The men spoke one by one. Uncle Arif said, "I know an old well in a valley to the north, but I haven't seen it for years, and I don't know exactly where the valley begins."

Basil was sitting behind his father. He wanted to speak, but he felt shy.

Abu Maher saw him and said, "And you, Basil? Tell us what you think."

Basil said in a quiet voice, "At sunset I saw flocks of sandgrouse all flying in that direction. My father says sandgrouse only fly like that toward water."

Abu Maher looked at Uncle Arif, and Arif said, "The direction the boy is talking about is the direction of the valley."

So at dawn they set off, following the sandgrouse, with Uncle Arif studying the ground, until they saw the entrance to the valley between two rocks.

At the bottom of the valley they found the old well, full of cool water.

The camels drank, the people filled their waterskins, and they laughed for the first time in days. Abu Maher patted Basil on the shoulder and said nothing.

The caravan reached the city safely. And on the way back, whenever Abu Maher had a decision to make, he gathered the caravan and asked them — and he never forgot to ask Basil.

﴿وَأَمْرُهُمْ شُورَىٰ بَيْنَهُمْ﴾

📖 Ash-Shura 38. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

surra.x:
Abu Tariq had an olive press at the edge of the village. In autumn people brought their olives to it, and merchants stopped there on their journeys.

Tariq was twelve years old. He helped his father with the big millstone, and he knew all the merchants by name.

At the end of autumn, a merchant named Abu Mundhir stayed with them. He had a leather pouch sealed with red wax.

He said to Abu Tariq, "I'm travelling to faraway lands, and I'd rather not carry this on the road. Keep it safe for me until I come back in the spring."

Abu Tariq took it and put it in a wooden chest in the corner of the house, saying, "This is an amanah — something left in our trust, Tariq. It isn't ours."

Then winter came, and Abu Tariq went off to work in a faraway village. He told his son, "You're the man of the house until I come back."

That year the winter was harsh. The cold went on and on and there was little work, so the oil in the jars ran low, and so did the flour.

Tariq's mother fed Tariq first, then ate whatever was left, saying she was not hungry.

One day Tariq's friend Ayham came over and saw the chest in the corner. He asked about it, and Tariq told him.

Ayham said, "There must be lots of money in it. Take a little, then put it back in the spring. Who'll ever know?"

Tariq looked at the pouch for a long time, with the red seal on it just as Abu Mundhir had left it. Then he said, "I'll know."

And he closed the chest.

His mother had heard them talking. When Ayham left, she said, "Well done, Tariq."

Then Tariq's mother went to her own chest and took out two silver bracelets that had been part of her wedding things. She handed them to him and said, "Sell these at the market, and buy flour with the money."

So Tariq walked through the snow to the market, sold the bracelets, and came back carrying a sack of flour on his back.

The winter passed like that. Then the snow melted, the land turned green, and Abu Tariq came home from his travels.

The very first thing he asked about was the pouch. Tariq opened the chest — and there it was in its place, with the seal on it just as before.

At the end of spring, Abu Mundhir came. When he saw the seal unbroken, he opened the pouch in front of them, and it was full of gold.

He asked about their winter, and Abu Tariq told him about the snow and the flour and the bracelets — and about Ayham.

Abu Mundhir was silent for a long time. Then he said, "I have passed through many villages, and I have never found a trust kept better than in this house."

Then he made Abu Tariq his partner in the olive-oil trade, and every time he passed by he would call Tariq "Keeper of the Pouch."

﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ يَأْمُرُكُمْ أَن تُؤَدُّوا الْأَمَانَاتِ إِلَىٰ أَهْلِهَا﴾

📖 An-Nisa' 58. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

raghif.x:
For days, snow had blocked the road to the village. The flour seller could not come up, and no one could go down.

The flour sack in Hadi's house grew lighter day by day, until Hadi could hear the bottom of it whenever his mother scooped from it.

On the evening of the fifth day, Hadi's mother took one single loaf out of the oven. Then she shook the sack over the dough bowl, and nothing came out.

She put the loaf on the tray between Hadi and Sumayya and said, "This is our dinner tonight, and the morning is in Allah's hands."

Hadi reached out for the loaf. He had been hungry since noon.

Before he could break it, there was a soft knock at the door.

Hadi opened it, and there was their neighbour Abu Subhi, an old man who lived alone at the end of the alley. His beard was white with snow, and his hands were trembling.

He said, "My son, do you have a piece of bread? I haven't tasted anything since yesterday."

Hadi looked at the loaf, and then at his mother.

His mother said in a quiet voice, "It's your loaf, Hadi. Do what you think is right."

Sumayya looked at the loaf and said nothing.

Hadi stood there for a long time. Then he picked up the tray and held it out to Abu Subhi.

The old man said, "And what about you?" Hadi said, "There are three of us to keep each other warm, and you're all alone."

Abu Subhi took the loaf, made a long du'a for them, and walked off through the snow to his house.

Then Hadi's mother brought out a little bundle with a handful of dried figs she had been saving. The three of them shared them, and went to sleep.

In the morning the men of the village dug a path through the snow, and the flour seller came up with his mule.

Abu Subhi got to him first, took out all the money he had in his pocket, and said, "The first sack goes to Hadi's house."

The seller brought the sack to Hadi's door, with Abu Subhi beside him leaning on his stick.

The old man said to Hadi's mother, "I had money but no bread. You had only one loaf, and you gave it away. So this is for that."

That morning, Hadi's mother kneaded lots and lots of dough, and she sent Hadi with the very first loaf out of the oven to Abu Subhi's house.

And from that day on, Hadi stopped by the old man's house every morning on his way.

﴿وَيُؤْثِرُونَ عَلَىٰ أَنفُسِهِمْ وَلَوْ كَانَ بِهِمْ خَصَاصَةٌ﴾

📖 Al-Hashr 9. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

dayf.x:
Dhiyab and his family lived in a house of hair — a tent woven from goat hair. It stood all alone at the edge of the desert, far from other people's homes, with a few sheep around it.

One winter night, heavy rain poured down, and the wind shook the ropes of the tent.

While they were sitting around the fire, they heard a camel kneel down outside, and then a man calling, "O people of the house!"

Abu Dhiyab went to the entrance and said, "May Allah greet you with peace — come in!"

In came a stranger, his clothes dripping with water. He had lost his way in the rain.

Dhiyab whispered to his mother, "We don't know him, Mama, and we only have a little food."

His mother said, "You don't ask a guest who he is until he has eaten and rested. That's how your father was, and how your grandfather was."

Abu Dhiyab seated the guest in the best place in the tent, close to the fire, and said to his son, "Get up, Dhiyab, and make the coffee."

Dhiyab got up to roast the coffee beans and then crush them in the mortar, while the guest held his hands out to the fire until his shivering stopped.

Then, from behind the curtain that separates the family from the guests, Umm Dhiyab brought out everything they had: dates in a dish, thin bread, and a little ghee.

Abu Dhiyab served it to the guest and sat eating with him, one small bite at a time, so that the guest would not feel shy, saying, "Eat — this home is your home."

Dhiyab watched the dish empty. He had been hoping to have his dinner from it.

Then he saw that the guest's clothes were wet. He got up and went to his farwa, which he slept in — a coat made of sheepskin with the wool still on it — and carried it over and put it around the man's shoulders.

His father looked at him and smiled.

The guest slept that night in the sheepskin coat by the fire, and Dhiyab slept wrapped in his father's cloak.

In the morning, when the rain had stopped, the guest tied his things onto his camel and said to Abu Dhiyab, "I am Rakan, from the people of the eastern valley. I owe you a night like this one."

Months went by. Then, in a harsh summer, Abu Dhiyab and his son went out looking for water and pasture. A sandstorm blew up on them, and they lost their way.

When the storm cleared, they saw tents in a valley and walked toward them, exhausted. A man came running out to them — and it was Rakan!

He took Dhiyab by the hand and said, "Welcome, owner of the sheepskin coat!"

Rakan gave them the best place in his home for three days and treated them with great honour. Then he showed them the way to water and pasture.

After that, whenever a guest came to them, Dhiyab was always the first to get up and make the coffee.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honour his guest."

📖 Agreed upon (Al-Bukhari and Muslim). This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

zeer.x:
Every morning Hajj Abdul-Sabour put a big clay jar on the market road, under a big tree. He filled it from the water pump, covered it with a wooden lid, and hung a cup on it.

He would say, "This is for the wayfarer — the traveller who passes by us with no water of his own."

One summer noon, Khalid and his two friends, Mahmoud and Sharif, were playing ball near the tree. Each of them had his own water bottle.

Khalid's bottle was big and new. He had filled it at home and had not drunk from it yet.

When Khalid got tired, he went to the jar, lifted the lid, and filled the cup.

Mahmoud said to him, "Why are you drinking from the jar, Khalid, when your bottle is full?"

Khalid said, "The jar's for whoever passes by, and I'm passing by! Besides, its water is colder."

Sharif said, "It's not haram to drink from it, but the Hajj put it there for people who don't have water — and we've got our own."

Khalid laughed and drank one cup, then another. Then he poured a cup over his head because of the heat, until the water in the jar was down to the bottom.

After Asr, Uncle Rizq came from the market. He was an old seller carrying a heavy box on his back, and he had been walking in the heat since morning.

He reached the jar, lifted the lid, and dipped in the cup — and only a few drops came out.

Uncle Rizq sat down in the shade of the tree, wiped the sweat from his forehead, and said nothing.

Mahmoud turned to Khalid and said quietly, "See? That's the wayfarer the jar was put there for."

Khalid was holding his full bottle, and his face had turned red.

Sharif said, "And your bottle is still full, Khalid."

Khalid got up, walked over to Uncle Rizq, and poured from his bottle into the cup until it was full. The man drank until his thirst was gone, and said, "May Allah give you water, my son, on the Day of thirst."

When Uncle Rizq had gone, Mahmoud said, "What about the jar? Someone else will pass by before Maghrib."

So they grabbed their three bottles and ran to the pump, filling them and running back to pour them into the jar, again and again.

At Maghrib, Hajj Abdul-Sabour came with his bucket and found the jar full, with the three boys around it, their clothes wet and panting for breath.

He asked them what had happened, and Khalid told him everything, hiding nothing. The Hajj smiled and patted their heads.

From that day on, the three boys got to the jar before the Hajj every morning and filled it before anyone passed by.

And whenever Khalid had water left in his bottle on the way home, he poured it into the jar.

﴿وَآتِ ذَا الْقُرْبَىٰ حَقَّهُ وَالْمِسْكِينَ وَابْنَ السَّبِيلِ﴾

📖 Al-Isra' 26. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

bab.x:
Joud loved all his neighbours, and they loved him. In the daytime the doors of the neighbourhood were never locked, so he walked in through them just as he walked into his own house.

He would go into his friend Taym's house, take his bike, and leave. He would go into Uncle Abu Nader's yard and pick figs from his fig tree — without asking anyone.

The neighbours would laugh and say, "Joud belongs to the whole neighbourhood."

But one day Taym went out and could not find his bike. He looked for it until evening, and then he saw it by Joud's door.

He did not say anything. He just went back into his house quietly.

One hot noon, Joud's ball flew into Abu Nader's yard. He pushed the door open and ran in as usual.

Uncle Abu Nader was asleep in the shade. Joud tripped over a clay water jug, and it broke. The old man woke up in fright, thinking it was a thief.

When Abu Nader saw that it was Joud, he calmed down, but his hand stayed on his chest for a while as he caught his breath.

Then he said to him calmly, "Joud, you're like a son to me. But a house has a door, and a door is for knocking."

Joud went out with his ball, his face burning.

When he got home, he told his grandmother what had happened. She said, "Did you know, Joud, that Allah mentions this in His Book?"

Then she recited: ﴿لَا تَدْخُلُوا بُيُوتًا غَيْرَ بُيُوتِكُمْ حَتَّىٰ تَسْتَأْنِسُوا وَتُسَلِّمُوا عَلَىٰ أَهْلِهَا﴾

And she said, "You knock, you say salam, and you wait until you're given permission."

Joud said, "And what if they don't give permission?" She said, "Then you go back, and you don't get upset. The person in the house might be asleep, or ill, or busy with something they don't want anyone to see."

Then she said, "Whatever you wouldn't like in your own home, don't do in other people's homes."

In the evening, Joud went into his room and found that his little sister Zeina had gone in while he was away. She had opened his box of colours and coloured all over his notebook.

He shouted, "Who said you could come in?!"

Then he suddenly went quiet, remembering Abu Nader's jug.

He sat down next to Zeina, gathered up the colours with her, and said, "Next time, knock on the door, and I'll open it for you."

Then he went out to the market and bought a clay jug with his pocket money.

When he reached Abu Nader's house, he found the door open as it was every day — but he did not go in. He stood at it, knocked three times, and said, "As-salamu alaykum, Uncle."

Abu Nader came, smiling, and said, "Wa alaykum as-salam. Come in, Joud." So he went in and handed him the jug.

Then he went to Taym's door, knocked, and said, "Taym, may I ride your bike?"

Taym laughed and said, "Since you asked permission, ride it — and I'll be right behind you!"

﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا لَا تَدْخُلُوا بُيُوتًا غَيْرَ بُيُوتِكُمْ حَتَّىٰ تَسْتَأْنِسُوا وَتُسَلِّمُوا عَلَىٰ أَهْلِهَا ۚ ذَٰلِكُمْ خَيْرٌ لَّكُمْ لَعَلَّكُمْ تَذَكَّرُونَ﴾

📖 An-Nur 27. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

janna.x:
Long, long ago, there was a good man who had a garden full of fruit, with palm trees and crops.

The scholars of tafsir mention that when harvest day came, he would open its gate to the poor, and each of them would take his share of what fell. And Allah blessed the garden for him.

When he died, his sons inherited the garden. They watched the poor coming every year, and they said, "Our father gave away too much. We have more right to our fruit."

So they agreed to pick all of it early in the morning, before people woke up.

﴿إِذْ أَقْسَمُوا لَيَصْرِمُنَّهَا مُصْبِحِينَ ۝ وَلَا يَسْتَثْنُونَ﴾

They swore an oath and did not say "In sha Allah," as if tomorrow were in their hands.

Then they slept peacefully that night, with the garden green under the moon.

In the night, a command from Allah came to the garden while they knew nothing.

﴿فَطَافَ عَلَيْهَا طَائِفٌ مِّن رَّبِّكَ وَهُمْ نَائِمُونَ ۝ فَأَصْبَحَتْ كَالصَّرِيمِ﴾

It became black and burnt, like the dark night, with no fruit and no leaves.

They got up before dawn, calling to one another: ﴿أَنِ اغْدُوا عَلَىٰ حَرْثِكُمْ إِن كُنتُمْ صَارِمِينَ﴾

Then they set off walking in the dark, speaking in low voices so that no one would hear them.

﴿فَانطَلَقُوا وَهُمْ يَتَخَافَتُونَ ۝ أَن لَّا يَدْخُلَنَّهَا الْيَوْمَ عَلَيْكُم مِّسْكِينٌ﴾

They walked along, sure that they could do what they wanted, and that they would come back with all the fruit for themselves alone.

﴿وَغَدَوْا عَلَىٰ حَرْدٍ قَادِرِينَ﴾

When they reached it, they stood there, unable to believe it. Where were the green trees? Where was the fruit?

They said, ﴿إِنَّا لَضَالُّونَ﴾ — "Maybe we took the wrong path, and this isn't our garden."

Then they looked around and recognised it, and they said: ﴿بَلْ نَحْنُ مَحْرُومُونَ﴾

Among them was one brother who was the fairest and wisest of them. He had warned them before, but they had not listened to him.

﴿قَالَ أَوْسَطُهُمْ أَلَمْ أَقُل لَّكُمْ لَوْلَا تُسَبِّحُونَ﴾

"Didn't I tell you: remember Allah, thank Him, and don't keep the poor from their right?"

They realised their mistake and said: ﴿سُبْحَانَ رَبِّنَا إِنَّا كُنَّا ظَالِمِينَ﴾

Then they turned to one another, each blaming his brother, and then they all said together: ﴿يَا وَيْلَنَا إِنَّا كُنَّا طَاغِينَ﴾

But they did not lose hope in Allah's mercy. They turned back to Him in repentance.

﴿عَسَىٰ رَبُّنَا أَن يُبْدِلَنَا خَيْرًا مِّنْهَا إِنَّا إِلَىٰ رَبِّنَا رَاغِبُونَ﴾

Wealth that is kept from the poor has no barakah in it — and repentance is a door that never closes.

📖 Their story is in Surat Al-Qalam, verses 17–33.

sabt.x:
There was a town of the Children of Israel by the seashore, whose people lived by fishing.

Allah had commanded them to stop fishing for one day each week — the Sabbath, Saturday — and to spend that day worshipping Him.

﴿وَاسْأَلْهُمْ عَنِ الْقَرْيَةِ الَّتِي كَانَتْ حَاضِرَةَ الْبَحْرِ﴾

Then Allah tested them, to see whether they would obey or disobey.

On the Sabbath the fish came to them in great numbers, right on the surface of the water, almost jumping onto the shore. But when Sunday came, they disappeared into the sea, and the people could not find any of them.

﴿إِذْ تَأْتِيهِمْ حِيتَانُهُمْ يَوْمَ سَبْتِهِمْ شُرَّعًا وَيَوْمَ لَا يَسْبِتُونَ ۙ لَا تَأْتِيهِمْ﴾

Some of them grew unhappy about this and said, "We won't fish on the Sabbath. But we'll dig pools by the shore, and when the fish swim into them on the Sabbath, we'll block them in, and take them on Sunday."

They thought they were obeying, but in truth they were playing a trick on Allah's command.

They did this week after week. Their houses filled up with fish, and they said, "We didn't catch them on the Sabbath!"

﴿كَذَٰلِكَ نَبْلُوهُم بِمَا كَانُوا يَفْسُقُونَ﴾

The people of the town split into three groups:

One group played the trick to catch fish. One group warned them and gave them good advice. And one group kept quiet — they neither did it nor tried to stop it.

The quiet group said to those giving advice: ﴿لِمَ تَعِظُونَ قَوْمًا ۙ اللَّهُ مُهْلِكُهُمْ أَوْ مُعَذِّبُهُمْ عَذَابًا شَدِيدًا﴾ — meaning, there's no use advising them.

The advisers answered: ﴿مَعْذِرَةً إِلَىٰ رَبِّكُمْ وَلَعَلَّهُمْ يَتَّقُونَ﴾

"We speak the truth so that our Lord knows we did not stay silent — and maybe they will come back."

But the tricksters did not come back. Instead, they went further and further.

﴿فَلَمَّا نَسُوا مَا ذُكِّرُوا بِهِ أَنجَيْنَا الَّذِينَ يَنْهَوْنَ عَنِ السُّوءِ وَأَخَذْنَا الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا بِعَذَابٍ بَئِيسٍ﴾

So Allah saved those who had tried to stop the wrongdoing, and punished those who had tricked and disobeyed.

﴿فَلَمَّا عَتَوْا عَن مَّا نُهُوا عَنْهُ قُلْنَا لَهُمْ كُونُوا قِرَدَةً خَاسِئِينَ﴾

Allah turned them into lowly apes — the punishment for those who thought they could fool Allah.

Then they died after a few days, and they left no children behind. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah has never given those who were transformed any children or descendants. Apes and pigs existed before that." (Narrated by Muslim)

So the apes we see today are a different creation that Allah made; they do not come from those people.

Tricking your way around Allah's command is disobedience, even if it is dressed up to look like obedience.

And whoever sees something wrong should say the truth gently, and never say, "There's no use." For those who warned were the ones who were saved.

📖 Their story is in Surat Al-A'raf, verses 163–166.

namla.x:
In a wide valley there were homes for ants under the ground, with more doors than anyone could count. The ants went in and out, carrying grain to their homes for the winter days.

Sulayman (peace be upon him) was a prophet and a king. Allah gave him power over things He gave to no one else: armies of people, of jinn, and of birds, marching in wonderful order.

﴿وَحُشِرَ لِسُلَيْمَانَ جُنُودُهُ مِنَ الْجِنِّ وَالْإِنسِ وَالطَّيْرِ فَهُمْ يُوزَعُونَ﴾

The army marched on until it came near the Valley of the Ants.

An ant felt it coming. The ground shook under her legs, she heard the sound of feet getting closer, and she saw the dust rising at the start of the valley.

She did not run away alone, and she did not say, "I'll save myself." Instead, she called out to her people:

﴿يَا أَيُّهَا النَّمْلُ ادْخُلُوا مَسَاكِنَكُمْ لَا يَحْطِمَنَّكُمْ سُلَيْمَانُ وَجُنُودُهُ﴾

Then she said words full of amazing fairness: ﴿وَهُمْ لَا يَشْعُرُونَ﴾

She did not accuse them of being cruel. She made an excuse for them: if they step on us, it won't be on purpose — they cannot see us.

The ants hurried into their homes, going in through every door, until not one of them was left on the ground.

The army passed through the valley, and not a single ant was crushed.

Sulayman (peace be upon him) heard what the ant said, for Allah had taught him the speech of birds and animals.

﴿فَتَبَسَّمَ ضَاحِكًا مِّن قَوْلِهَا﴾

He smiled at her wisdom, at how she cared for her people, and at how fair she was.

And he was not proud of his kingdom or his armies. Instead, he raised his hands, thanking Allah:

﴿رَبِّ أَوْزِعْنِي أَنْ أَشْكُرَ نِعْمَتَكَ الَّتِي أَنْعَمْتَ عَلَيَّ وَعَلَىٰ وَالِدَيَّ وَأَنْ أَعْمَلَ صَالِحًا تَرْضَاهُ وَأَدْخِلْنِي بِرَحْمَتِكَ فِي عِبَادِكَ الصَّالِحِينَ﴾

A little ant who cared for her people and warned them, and made excuses for others. And a great king who heard her and thanked his Lord, and was not arrogant.

📖 Her story is in Surat An-Naml, verses 17–19.

yasin.x:
There was once a city whose people worshipped idols. Allah sent them two messengers, calling them to worship Him alone, but they called them liars. So He sent a third to support them.

﴿إِذْ أَرْسَلْنَا إِلَيْهِمُ اثْنَيْنِ فَكَذَّبُوهُمَا فَعَزَّزْنَا بِثَالِثٍ فَقَالُوا إِنَّا إِلَيْكُم مُّرْسَلُونَ﴾

The people of the city said: ﴿مَا أَنتُمْ إِلَّا بَشَرٌ مِّثْلُنَا﴾

The messengers said: ﴿رَبُّنَا يَعْلَمُ إِنَّا إِلَيْكُمْ لَمُرْسَلُونَ ۝ وَمَا عَلَيْنَا إِلَّا الْبَلَاغُ الْمُبِينُ﴾ — meaning, our job is only to deliver the message to you, and guidance comes from Allah.

The people grew angry and said: ﴿إِنَّا تَطَيَّرْنَا بِكُمْ﴾ — meaning, "You have brought us nothing but bad luck." Then they threatened them:

﴿لَئِن لَّمْ تَنتَهُوا لَنَرْجُمَنَّكُمْ وَلَيَمَسَّنَّكُم مِّنَّا عَذَابٌ أَلِيمٌ﴾

At the far end of the city, in its most distant corner, there lived a man who believed in Allah. When he heard that his people wanted to harm the messengers, he did not wait. He came running — hurrying as fast as he could — to speak the word of truth.

﴿وَجَاءَ مِنْ أَقْصَى الْمَدِينَةِ رَجُلٌ يَسْعَىٰ﴾

He stood among his people and said: ﴿يَا قَوْمِ اتَّبِعُوا الْمُرْسَلِينَ ۝ اتَّبِعُوا مَن لَّا يَسْأَلُكُمْ أَجْرًا وَهُم مُّهْتَدُونَ﴾

Look at them: they don't ask you for money or for fame, and they are calling you to what is good.

Then he spoke to them gently about himself, as if he were talking to himself so that they would hear:

﴿وَمَا لِيَ لَا أَعْبُدُ الَّذِي فَطَرَنِي وَإِلَيْهِ تُرْجَعُونَ﴾

How could I not worship the One who created me? And you too will all return to Him.

﴿أَأَتَّخِذُ مِن دُونِهِ آلِهَةً إِن يُرِدْنِ الرَّحْمَٰنُ بِضُرٍّ لَّا تُغْنِ عَنِّي شَفَاعَتُهُمْ شَيْئًا وَلَا يُنقِذُونِ﴾

Idols that cannot hear and cannot help — how could I worship them?

Then he declared it openly in front of them all: ﴿إِنِّي آمَنتُ بِرَبِّكُمْ فَاسْمَعُونِ﴾

His people could not bear his words, and they killed him.

But Allah honoured him, and his reward was Jannah. ﴿قِيلَ ادْخُلِ الْجَنَّةَ﴾

When he saw how Allah had honoured him, he held no grudge against the people who had killed him. Instead, he wished they could know, so that they would believe:

﴿قَالَ يَا لَيْتَ قَوْمِي يَعْلَمُونَ ۝ بِمَا غَفَرَ لِي رَبِّي وَجَعَلَنِي مِنَ الْمُكْرَمِينَ﴾

He gave them good advice while he was alive, and he wished them good even after his death.

One man, who came from the farthest place, and who was not a messenger. But he heard the truth, and he stood up for it, and he did not stay silent.

📖 His story is in Surat Ya-Sin, verses 13–27.

rabbayani.x:
Every Thursday, Grandpa Uthman carried Idris on his shoulders to the market, while little Idris laughed and tugged at his turban.

When they reached the sweet seller, Grandpa put him down and bought him a piece of sesame candy. Then he lifted him up again and carried him back up the road.

The years went by. Idris turned eleven and became so fast he could outrun the wind, while Grandpa Uthman now walked with a stick, step by step, stopping on the road to rest.

But he still went to the market every Thursday, and he still took Idris with him.

One Thursday, Idris saw his friend Ilyas at the end of the road, playing ball with the other boys.

He said to his grandfather, "You walk slowly, Grandpa, and the boys are waiting for me. I'll get to the market before you." And he ran off before he could hear the answer.

Idris played until he forgot the time. Then Ilyas said to him, "Isn't your grandpa with you?"

Idris turned around and saw his grandfather far away by the stone steps. His stick had fallen, and he was trying to bend down to it but could not.

Idris ran to him, picked up the stick, and gave it to his grandfather.

Grandpa smiled and said, "It's all right, my boy. The steps have grown taller than they used to be." And he was out of breath.

On the way back, they passed the little river. Grandpa stopped and said, "Do you remember, Idris? Once, when you were small, a flood came. I carried you on my shoulder and waded through water up to my knees until I got you home."

Idris was quiet. He did not remember — but he believed it.

When they got home, he asked his mother, "Did Grandpa carry me a lot?"

She said, "He used to carry you until you fell asleep on his shoulder, and he wouldn't put you down until you woke up."

That night, Idris lay thinking for a long time before he fell asleep. Then he remembered an ayah he had memorised in his Quran circle:

﴿وَقُل رَّبِّ ارْحَمْهُمَا كَمَا رَبَّيَانِي صَغِيرًا﴾

And he understood it for the first time.

The next Thursday, Idris took his grandfather's basket, gave him his arm, and walked beside him, step by step.

When Ilyas saw him and called him to play, he said, "I'll join you after the market — I'm with my grandpa."

When they reached the sweet seller, Idris took out of his pocket a coin he had saved, and bought his grandfather some sesame candy.

Grandpa laughed until tears came to his eyes, and said, "Now you're the one carrying me, Idris."

﴿وَاخْفِضْ لَهُمَا جَنَاحَ الذُّلِّ مِنَ الرَّحْمَةِ وَقُل رَّبِّ ارْحَمْهُمَا كَمَا رَبَّيَانِي صَغِيرًا﴾

📖 Al-Isra' 24. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

tamr.x:
Abu Mahdi had a stall in the date market, where he sold small boxes of dates from his own palm trees.

After school, Mahdi stood with him, arranging the dates in the boxes and calling out to people passing by.

One day his father went to pray and left him alone. On the stall was a box of small, dry dates that no one had bought since morning.

Mahdi said to himself, "If I put some big, shiny ones on top, it would sell in no time."

So he emptied half the box, put the dry dates at the bottom, and stacked the biggest, shiniest dates on top.

His friend Diya came by, saw it, and said, "What's this, Mahdi? Whoever buys it will find dry dates under the sweet ones."

Mahdi said, "This is business. Everybody does it."

Then Uncle Ayyub came along, a poor old man from the neighbourhood. He looked at the box and said, "How lovely! My grandson is ill, and dates are the only thing he'll eat."

He counted the coins from his palm one by one, gave them to Mahdi, picked up the box, and left.

When Abu Mahdi came back, he found the box had been sold and asked about it. Mahdi said, "Allah sold it for us."

But he said it without looking his father in the eye.

The next morning, Uncle Ayyub came back with the box. He was not angry — he was sad.

He said, "My son, my grandson ate the dates on top and was happy. Then he reached in and found the rest dry and too hard to eat. I thought you were honest."

Mahdi's face turned red, and he could not speak.

Diya, who was standing with him, said, "Tell him, Mahdi."

Mahdi raised his head and said, "I did it, Uncle. Please forgive me."

Abu Mahdi took the box of dry dates, filled it with their very best dates, and gave it back to Uncle Ayyub, along with his money.

Then, after the old man had gone, he said to his son, "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Whoever cheats us is not one of us.' Would you like not to be one of his people, Mahdi?"

That night, Mahdi sat sorting the dates: the big sweet ones in some boxes, and the small dry ones in other boxes for a lower price.

He told his father, "Whoever wants the cheap ones will know what he's buying, and whoever wants the expensive ones will know what he's buying."

Soon people in the market were saying, "Buy from Mahdi's stall — what you see on top is what you'll find at the bottom."

And every week Uncle Ayyub came by and bought a box for his grandson, without even checking inside.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever cheats us is not one of us."

📖 Narrated by Muslim. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

kabir.x:
It was Eid morning, and the whole big family had gathered in the sitting room: the uncles, the sons, and the little grandchildren.

Hamza came in wearing his new clothes. He saw that the seat at the head of the room was empty, so he sat in it and stretched out his legs.

Then the plate of sweets came round. Hamza reached out before everyone else and picked the biggest piece.

His little cousin Jumana was looking at the plate. When she reached out her hand, he told her, "Wait — you're little."

Jumana pulled her hand back and sat quietly.

Then Grandpa came in, leaning on his stick. He looked for his place at the head of the room, and found Hamza sitting in it.

He did not say anything. He sat down at the edge of the room, near the door.

Hamza's cousin Usama, who was twelve, got up, took his grandfather's hand, and said, "Your place is here, Grandpa."

Hamza got out of the seat, not happy about it, while Grandpa smiled at Usama and made du'a for him.

Then Usama took the plate of sweets. He started with Grandpa, then came to Jumana, bent down to her, and said, "You choose first. Which piece would you like?"

Jumana was delighted, and she chose a piece with a sugar rose on top.

When the children went out into the courtyard, Hamza whispered to Usama, "Why did you do that? The seat was empty, and the sweets are for whoever gets there first."

Usama said, "We respect our elders, and we are gentle with the little ones. That's what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said."

Hamza went quiet. He looked through the door at his grandfather at the head of the room, laughing with everyone.

Then he looked at Jumana in the courtyard, showing the sugar rose to her big brother and saying, "Usama let me choose first!"

That afternoon the children went out to the swing. There was only one, and they all gathered around it.

When it was Hamza's turn, he looked at Jumana standing at the very back and said, "Come on, Jumana, you go before me."

Grandpa put his hand on Hamza's head and said, "May Allah bless you, Hamza."

That was the sweetest du'a Hamza heard that whole Eid — sweeter than all the sweets.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "He is not one of us who does not show mercy to our young and respect to our elders."

📖 Narrated by At-Tirmidhi. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

Then he started drawing with it at home, until he almost thought it was his own.

Mu'adh would look at his box and see the empty space where the gold pencil belonged — but he felt too shy to ask his friend for it.

Ghaith shouted, "That's my eraser! You took it and never gave it back!"

Yahya said, "I thought you'd forgotten about it."

Ghaith suddenly went quiet. He put his hand on his school bag and felt the gold pencil inside it.

And he remembered Mu'adh's face as he looked at his box.

On the paper was a little drawing: a golden sun, and under it, "Thank you, my friend."

Mu'adh laughed and said, "I knew you'd bring it back."

Then he said, "You know what? The sun you drew is even nicer than the pencil itself."

Amina's grandmother wove carpets on a big wooden loom — a frame with threads stretched across it — in a corner of the house. Every evening Amina sat beside her, watching her fingers as she tied the knots.

One day she said, "Teach me, Grandma."

So her grandmother set up a little loom for her, gave her some red wool, and said, "One knot at a time, one row at a time. A rug isn't woven in a day."

Amina worked fast. She tied twenty knots in an hour and got up, very pleased.

Her grandmother looked at the weaving. The row was crooked and the knots were loose, so she calmly undid all of it and said, "Start again."

Amina sat down again. She tied knots and hurried, and the row went crooked a second time, and her grandmother undid it.

Amina cried and said, "I'll never learn! You weave so fast, and I can't do it."

Her grandmother went to an old chest and took out a small rug with faded colours and slightly crooked rows.

She said, "This is the first rug I ever wove, when I was your age. I wove it for a whole winter, and my mother undid it more times than I can count."

Then she said, "Speed comes from patience — not patience from speed. Ask Allah for help, count your knots, and don't look at the end of the rug."

Amina went back to her loom. Now she tied each knot and then pulled it tight, counting in a whisper, and she did not get up until the row was straight.

A single row took her a whole evening.

The winter went by like that. There was snow on the mountains, fire in the stove, and every evening the rows of red wool grew a little higher.

On some nights she got tired and left the loom, and then came back to it the next day.

When spring came, her grandmother cut the last threads, shook out the little rug, and spread it on the floor.

It was red, with straight rows, and in the middle was a little yellow star that Amina had woven all by herself.

Amina spread it in the spot where her grandmother prayed and said, "This is for you, Grandma — my first rug."

Her grandmother sat down on it and stroked the yellow star. She did not say anything, but her eyes were smiling.

﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا اسْتَعِينُوا بِالصَّبْرِ وَالصَّلَاةِ ۚ إِنَّ اللَّهَ مَعَ الصَّابِرِينَ﴾

📖 Al-Baqarah 153. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

Yusuf jumped over after him, and they went on to school.

Yusuf said, "Shouldn't we move it, Suhaib?"

Suhaib said, "We didn't throw it there, so why should we move it? Whoever it belongs to can pick it up."

He did not see the branch. He tripped over it and fell on his side, and the thorns scratched his leg.

Suhaib and Yusuf were on their way back from school. They ran to him, helped him up, and brushed the dust off his clothes.

Uncle Na'im said, rubbing his leg, "It's all right, boys. But whoever moves this branch will have a great reward."

Then he told them, "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'While a man was walking along a road, he found a thorny branch on the road and moved it aside, so Allah thanked him and forgave him.'"

Suhaib looked at Yusuf, and Yusuf looked at Suhaib.

Then Suhaib said quietly, "Yusuf wanted to move it yesterday… and I said no."

Suhaib wrapped his hands in the end of his bag, and Yusuf took hold of the other end. Together they dragged the branch off the road and threw it into the field.

Then they gathered the stones the storm had rolled onto the road and put them at the side.

Uncle Na'im walked along the road, which was now clear, and smiled, saying, "Now I can walk without being afraid."

And he made du'a for them all the way to the masjid.

From that day on, Suhaib walked to school with his eyes on the ground. Whenever he saw a stone, or broken glass, or thorns, he moved it off the road.

And Yusuf would say, "Now you see the road better than I do!"

📖 Agreed upon (Al-Bukhari and Muslim). This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

Ammar sat next to Salman in class. He had the neatest handwriting of all the boys, and he was the quietest.

Salman noticed that Ammar wrote with a very short pencil, and that his notebook had run out of pages, so he wrote in the margins.

At break time Ammar had no food. He would sit and say, "I'm not hungry."

Then Salman found out that Ammar's father was ill and had not been able to work for months.

Salman told his father, and his father asked, "What would you like to do?"

He said, "Give him some of my pocket money. But I'm afraid he'll feel embarrassed in front of me, or that the other boys will find out and laugh at him."

His father said, "Then give to him without him knowing it's from you. The best sadaqah is the kind where your left hand doesn't know what your right hand gave."

Then he gave him some money, and Salman added some of his own pocket money on top.

Salman bought new notebooks and pencils and put them in a bag with no name on it.

Early in the morning, before anyone arrived, he put the bag in Ammar's desk, then went out to the playground as if he had never been inside.

When Ammar opened his desk, he found the bag. He looked around in surprise, then read a little note inside: "From a brother who loves you for the sake of Allah."

Ammar smiled — and he had no idea who it was.

Every week after that, Salman left something in Ammar's desk: a wrapped sandwich, or a pencil, or a notebook.

At break time, Bilal said, "Do you know who's leaving things for Ammar? I want to find out!"

Salman said, "What's it got to do with us? If he wanted people to know, he'd have written his name."

Then he changed the subject to football.

Months later, Ammar's father got better and went back to work. Ammar came to class happy, carrying a bag of sweets, and handed them out to all the boys.

He said, "These are for everyone who stood by me… and for the brother I don't know, if he's one of you."

Salman took his piece and said, "May Allah reward him with good, whoever he is."

﴿إِن تُبْدُوا الصَّدَقَاتِ فَنِعِمَّا هِيَ ۖ وَإِن تُخْفُوهَا وَتُؤْتُوهَا الْفُقَرَاءَ فَهُوَ خَيْرٌ لَّكُمْ﴾

📖 Al-Baqarah 271. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

baqara.x:
Among the Children of Israel, a man was killed, and no one knew who had killed him.

The people argued about it, and each group accused the other, until the trouble between them almost grew out of control.

﴿وَإِذْ قَتَلْتُمْ نَفْسًا فَادَّارَأْتُمْ فِيهَا ۖ وَاللَّهُ مُخْرِجٌ مَّا كُنتُمْ تَكْتُمُونَ﴾

So they went to their prophet, Musa (peace be upon him), asking him to pray to Allah so they could find out who the killer was.

He said to them: ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ يَأْمُرُكُمْ أَن تَذْبَحُوا بَقَرَةً﴾

An easy command: any cow they slaughtered would have been enough.

But they were surprised and said: ﴿أَتَتَّخِذُنَا هُزُوًا﴾ — meaning, "Are you making fun of us? We ask you about the killer, and you tell us to slaughter a cow!"

He said: ﴿أَعُوذُ بِاللَّهِ أَنْ أَكُونَ مِنَ الْجَاهِلِينَ﴾ — for a prophet would never make fun of anyone.

If they had slaughtered any cow at all, that would have been the end of it. But they came back asking:

﴿ادْعُ لَنَا رَبَّكَ يُبَيِّن لَّنَا مَا هِيَ﴾

And the answer came: ﴿لَّا فَارِضٌ وَلَا بِكْرٌ عَوَانٌ بَيْنَ ذَٰلِكَ﴾ — meaning, not old and not young, but in between.

That was not enough for them, and they came back asking: ﴿مَا لَوْنُهَا﴾?

And the answer came: ﴿إِنَّهَا بَقَرَةٌ صَفْرَاءُ فَاقِعٌ لَّوْنُهَا تَسُرُّ النَّاظِرِينَ﴾

A bright, bright yellow, that makes everyone who sees it happy.

Then they asked a third time: ﴿ادْعُ لَنَا رَبَّكَ يُبَيِّن لَّنَا مَا هِيَ إِنَّ الْبَقَرَ تَشَابَهَ عَلَيْنَا﴾

And every time they asked, things became harder for them, and fewer cows would do.

And the answer came: a cow that had never been used to plough the land or to water the crops, healthy, with no other colour on it but its own.

﴿إِنَّهَا بَقَرَةٌ لَّا ذَلُولٌ تُثِيرُ الْأَرْضَ وَلَا تَسْقِي الْحَرْثَ مُسَلَّمَةٌ لَّا شِيَةَ فِيهَا﴾

They said: ﴿الْآنَ جِئْتَ بِالْحَقِّ﴾

They searched for a long time, and the only cow they could find with all these qualities belonged to a poor young man who was very good to his mother.

The scholars of tafsir mention that they had to buy it from him for a great deal of money — because they had made things hard for themselves, so Allah made things hard for them.

﴿فَذَبَحُوهَا وَمَا كَادُوا يَفْعَلُونَ﴾

Then Allah commanded them to strike the dead man with a part of the cow, and Allah brought him back to life for a moment, and he told them who had killed him.

﴿كَذَٰلِكَ يُحْيِي اللَّهُ الْمَوْتَىٰ وَيُرِيكُمْ آيَاتِهِ لَعَلَّكُمْ تَعْقِلُونَ﴾

If they had slaughtered the very first cow, it would have been enough. But they asked too many questions about things they had not been asked to do, and they made something easy hard for themselves.

So when you are told to do something good, hurry to do it, and don't ask lots of questions that are of no use.

📖 Their story is in Surat Al-Baqarah, verses 67–73.

ibnay.x:
Adam (peace be upon him) had two sons. One of them looked after sheep, and the other farmed the land.

In those days the earth was wide and empty, with only one family of people living on it.

Allah commanded them both to offer a sacrifice — a gift to bring them closer to Allah.

The shepherd chose the best ram he had — the fattest one, and the one he loved most.

But the farmer gathered a bundle of the worst of his crops — things he did not want for himself.

Each of them placed his offering on the top of a mountain.

Allah accepted the offering from one of them and did not accept it from the other.

The scholars of tafsir mention that a fire came down from the sky and took the shepherd's offering, while the farmer's offering stayed on the ground.

The farmer's heart filled with envy and anger, and he said to his brother: ﴿لَأَقْتُلَنَّكَ﴾

His brother answered him calmly: ﴿إِنَّمَا يَتَقَبَّلُ اللَّهُ مِنَ الْمُتَّقِينَ﴾ — meaning, make your heart good, and your offering will be accepted.

Then he said: ﴿لَئِن بَسَطتَ إِلَيَّ يَدَكَ لِتَقْتُلَنِي مَا أَنَا بِبَاسِطٍ يَدِيَ إِلَيْكَ لِأَقْتُلَكَ ۖ إِنِّي أَخَافُ اللَّهَ رَبَّ الْعَالَمِينَ﴾

He did not answer anger with anger, because he feared Allah.

But envy took over the farmer, and he killed his brother.

﴿فَطَوَّعَتْ لَهُ نَفْسُهُ قَتْلَ أَخِيهِ فَقَتَلَهُ فَأَصْبَحَ مِنَ الْخَاسِرِينَ﴾

It was the very first time a human being was killed on earth.

He carried his brother, not knowing what to do with him, for he had never seen a dead person before.

Then Allah sent a crow, digging in the ground with its beak and its feet, to show him how to bury his brother.

﴿فَبَعَثَ اللَّهُ غُرَابًا يَبْحَثُ فِي الْأَرْضِ﴾

When he saw the crow, he said: ﴿يَا وَيْلَتَا أَعَجَزْتُ أَنْ أَكُونَ مِثْلَ هَٰذَا الْغُرَابِ فَأُوَارِيَ سَوْءَةَ أَخِي﴾

﴿فَأَصْبَحَ مِنَ النَّادِمِينَ﴾ — but only after his brother was gone, when regret could no longer help.

📖 Their story is in Surat Al-Ma'idah, verses 27–32.

📖 Agreed upon (Al-Bukhari and Muslim). This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

waqt.x:

He wrote on a piece of paper: Learn to swim. Memorise Juz' Amma. Make a wooden car.

But on the first day he said, "I'll play on the tablet for just one hour, and then I'll start."

All the weeks went by like that: "Tomorrow"… "Tomorrow"…

And the paper where he had written what he wanted to do stayed under the chair, covered in dust.

At the end of the holidays, Uncle Hasan invited the children of the street to his workshop to see what Wisam had made.

There was a wooden car with wheels that turned, a door that opened, and shiny red paint.

Wisam said, "And I learned to swim at the club in the mornings, and I memorised half of Juz' Amma with my dad after Isha."

Hani looked at his empty hands and said nothing.

Uncle Hasan saw him. He sat him down beside him and said, "Hani, the holiday wasn't any shorter for you than for Wisam. You both had exactly the same time."

Then he said, "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'There are two blessings that many people lose out on: good health and free time.'"

Hani said, "What does 'lose out' mean?" He said, "It's like someone who sells something precious for a cheap price. You sold your days for games that leave nothing behind."

Hani was quiet — and he understood.

That night he took the paper out from under the chair, blew the dust off it, and put the tablet away in a drawer.

Then under each thing he wrote a time: after Fajr, after Asr, after Isha.

When the next holidays came, Hani did not say "tomorrow." He went with Wisam to the workshop every afternoon, until he had made a wooden train for his little brother.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "There are two blessings that many people lose out on: good health and free time."

📖 Narrated by Al-Bukhari. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

fawq.x:

Sami looked at him and said to his friend, "He's little, and he doesn't go to a school like ours. What's he going to teach us?"

Jawad walked them through the olive trees. Sami said, "I know everything about trees. I read about them in my book."

Jawad said, "This tree is thirsty." Sami laughed. "How would you know? Trees can't talk."

Jawad said, "Its leaves are curled up, and its soil is dry and cracked." He dug his finger into the soil, and it was as dry as stone.

When the farmer came, he said, "Jawad's right. We forgot to water it days ago."

Then they came to the little river. Sami wanted to cross it by stepping on a shiny green stone.

Jawad shouted, "No! That stone has slippery moss on it!" But Sami would not listen to him.

His foot slipped, he fell into the water, and his book flew out of his hands and got soaking wet.

Jawad held out his hand and pulled him out, then fished out the book — and he did not laugh at him.

Sami sat in the sun drying his clothes, and Jawad sat down beside him.

Sami asked him quietly, "Who taught you all of this?" He said, "My grandfather — and the field itself. I learn something from it every day."

Then Jawad said, "And you know things I don't know. Do you know the name of the bright star that comes out at sunset?"

Sami laughed for the first time without any pride, and said, "I do — and I'll teach you."

When they got on the bus to go home, Mr Walid, the teacher, said, "What was the best thing you learned today, Sami?"

Sami said, "That someone who doesn't go to my school might know things I don't."

From that day on, Sami never raised his hand before the question was finished, and he listened to other people's answers just as he liked people to listen to his.

muhra.x:

Adnan was overjoyed, and he wanted to ride her that very same day.
