Shahba took fright and reared up on her back legs, and Adnan fell onto the sand.

He got up angry, fetched a stick, and said, "I'll teach her to obey!"

When Shahba saw the stick, she ran to the far end of the pen and would not let him come near her.

His little sister Lujain was watching from behind the fence. She said, "Adnan, she's scared of you, not stubborn."

Adnan said, "And what do you know about horses?"

Every day Adnan pulled and shouted, and Shahba shied away and kept her distance.

And every afternoon Lujain came with a handful of dates. She stood quietly by the fence and did not come closer.

After some days, Shahba came closer to Lujain step by step, and then ate the dates from her palm.

Lujain gently stroked her neck and spoke to her in a calm voice.

Grandpa saw them. He sat Adnan down beside him and said, "My son, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Allah is gentle, and He loves gentleness in all things.'"

Then he said, "Gentleness opens what a stick can never open."

Adnan threw the stick away and asked his sister, "Teach me, Lujain."

She said, "Don't shout, and don't pull. Stand close, and wait until she comes to you."

So every afternoon Adnan stood by the fence, with dates in his palm and patience in his heart.

Until one day Shahba came, ate from his hand, and rested her head on his shoulder.

A month later, Adnan rode Shahba around the farm. She walked slowly with him on her back, and Lujain walked beside her holding the rope.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah is gentle, and He loves gentleness in all things."

📖 Agreed upon (Al-Bukhari and Muslim). This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

mawid.x:
That winter, Lu'ay's mother was ill, so Lu'ay carried water from the well every morning, and his two jars were heavy for him.

His friend Marwan said to him, "I'll help you. I'll wait for you at the well tomorrow at dawn."

When morning came, Marwan got out of bed and found it bitterly cold, while his bed was so warm.

He said to himself, "If I slept a little longer… Lu'ay wouldn't be upset." Then he remembered that he had promised, and he got up.

He found Lu'ay at the well waiting for him, his hands red with cold.

They pulled up the bucket together, filled both jars, and each of them carried one.

It became an everyday thing. Marwan would say, "We meet at the well at dawn," and he was never late.

Then came a Sunday with no school.

On Saturday evening, two boys from the neighbourhood came to Marwan with a paper kite and said, "Tomorrow at dawn we're going out to the valley — the wind is strong there. Come with us!"

Marwan was thrilled and said, "Yes!"

When he went inside, he remembered Lu'ay and the well. He sat there torn: the valley and the kite on one side, and the two jars on the other.

He said, "Lu'ay can carry the water by himself for one day."

But he remembered that Lu'ay did not know about the trip, and that he would stand at the well in the cold, waiting for him.

And he remembered an ayah their teacher had recited: ﴿وَأَوْفُوا بِالْعَهْدِ ۖ إِنَّ الْعَهْدَ كَانَ مَسْئُولًا﴾

So he went out to the two boys and said, "I have a meeting at dawn that I can't miss. You go, and I'll catch up with you afterwards."

They said, "What meeting is that?" So he told them.

At dawn Marwan went to the well — and the two boys came with him, saying, "We'll fill the jars together, and then we'll all go to the valley."

The four of them filled the two jars in minutes.

Then they carried the water to Lu'ay's house, and they all went out to the valley and flew the kite until noon.

And Lu'ay would say, "I've never seen a friend who keeps his word like Marwan."

﴿وَأَوْفُوا بِالْعَهْدِ ۖ إِنَّ الْعَهْدَ كَانَ مَسْئُولًا﴾

📖 Al-Isra' 34. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

saa.x:
During the holidays, Bassam worked for Uncle Zakariyya, the watch repairer in the old market.

He loved the sound of all the clocks on the wall, ticking together as if they were talking.

Uncle Zakariyya worked slowly. He would open a watch, clean every piece inside it, and tighten every tiny screw until it was firm. Then he would listen to it for a long time before closing it.

Bassam would say to himself, "Why does he take so long?"

One day Uncle Zakariyya went out to pray, and a man came in with a watch that had stopped. He said, "I need it in an hour — I'm travelling."

Bassam said, "I'll fix it for you."

Bassam opened it quickly and moved its hands, and they turned. So he closed it without tightening the tiny screw inside it, and said, "Done!"

The man took it happily and left.

When Uncle Zakariyya came back, he looked at the table and saw the tiny screw lying on it.

He said, "Where's the watch this came out of, Bassam?"

In the evening the man came back angry, holding the watch, which had stopped. He said, "It stopped on the way, and I nearly missed my train!"

Bassam's face turned red, and he lowered his head.

Uncle Zakariyya apologised to the man and fixed the watch slowly in front of him, and did not charge him anything.

Then, after the man had gone, he said to Bassam, "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Allah loves that when one of you does a job, he does it well.'"

Then he said, "Quick, unfinished work has to be done twice. Work done well only has to be done once."

Bassam said, "Teach me to work like you."

So Bassam began opening the watches slowly, counting their pieces, tightening every screw, and listening to them before closing them.

It took him time — but not one of the watches he fixed ever came back to him.

A month later, the same man came back with his father's old watch and said, "I want Bassam to fix it."

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah has prescribed excellence in everything."

📖 Narrated by Muslim. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

basma.x:
Shahd was a kind girl, but she always walked around frowning, as if she were carrying something heavy on her shoulders.

Her friend Dana smiled at everyone she met, young or old.

In the morning they got on the bus, and Dana said to the driver with a smile, "Good morning, Uncle Jamil!"

Uncle Jamil smiled and said, "Good morning to you, my dear." But Shahd just sat down and did not look at him.

At school they passed Auntie Umm Sa'id, who had been cleaning the yard since dawn.

Dana said to her, "Jazakillahu khayran, Auntie — the yard looks lovely." Umm Sa'id lifted her head, and you could see the tiredness melting from her face.

Shahd said to Dana, "Why do you smile at everyone? You don't even know them."

Dana said, "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Your smile in your brother's face is a sadaqah for you.' And it's a sadaqah that doesn't cost me anything."

Shahd said, "A sadaqah? Without money?" Dana said, "Try it for just one day."

Shahd was quiet. She did not say yes, and she did not say no.

The next day Shahd got on the bus. She wanted to say good morning, but the words came out softly, and her smile was small.

Uncle Jamil said, "Good morning to you, Shahd! That's the first time I've seen you smile."

Then she passed Auntie Umm Sa'id and said to her, "As-salamu alaykum, Auntie." Umm Sa'id returned her salam happily and said, "Welcome, my dear!"

And Shahd felt something light in her chest.

At break time, a new girl was standing alone, not knowing anyone.

Shahd went over to her, smiled at her, and said, "Come and join us."

When Shahd got home, she told her mother, "Today I smiled five times — and five people smiled back at me."

Then she laughed and said, "And Dana does this every single day!"

From that day on, Uncle Jamil would say, "Now there are two smiles on my bus."

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Your smile in your brother's face is a sadaqah for you."

📖 Narrated by At-Tirmidhi. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

ghurfa.x:
Sara and her big sister Tala shared one room. Tala's half was tidy and clean, and Sara's half looked as if a storm had blown through it.

Clothes on the bed, books under it, and pencils everywhere.

Tala would say, "Tidy up your things, Sara." And Sara would say, "I know where everything is, so there's no need to tidy."

On the morning of the exam, Sara woke up late. She looked for her maths notebook, but she could not find it.

She turned over the clothes and the books while time ticked by and the bus was waiting.

Then she looked for her shoes and found only one. She found the other under the bed, along with a sock and an old piece of biscuit.

She sat down on the floor and cried.

Tala came in and sat down beside her. She reached up to her tidy shelf and gave Sara her own old notebook to revise from.

Then she found Sara's notebook in one minute, between the pillow and the wall.

In the evening Tala said, "Do you know, Sara, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Allah is beautiful, and He loves beauty.'"

Then she said, "And a tidy room is beautiful. It makes things easier for you before it makes them easier for anyone else."

Sara said, "But tidying takes so long, and I don't know where to start."

Tala said, "We'll start with something small: everything has its place, and when you take something, you put it back in its place."

So they tidied up together: the clothes in the wardrobe, the books on the shelf, the pencils in a box, and the shoes by the door.

Sara laughed every time she found something she had lost weeks ago.

When they had finished, Sara looked at the room. Her half was just like Tala's half — clean and tidy.

She said, "It's like a brand-new room!"

The next morning, Sara found her notebook and her shoes in a moment, and got to the bus before everyone else.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah is beautiful, and He loves beauty."

📖 Narrated by Muslim. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

ard.x:
Grandpa Abdul-Rahim had an olive grove on the hillside. Its trees had been planted by his grandfather's grandfather, and their trunks were twisted like the hands of old men.

He used to tell his grandson Yamen, "This land is an amanah, a trust. We inherited it from our fathers, and we will leave it to our children."

Every autumn Yamen went with his grandfather to pick the olives, and heard from him the story of each tree: this one his father planted on the day he was born; this one held on through a whole year of thirst.

One day some strangers came to the edge of the grove, carrying papers and maps. They said, "This land is ours now. Leave it."

Grandpa said in a steady voice, "This is the land of my fathers, and it has olive trees older than all of you."

When night came, the strangers cut down three trees at the edge of the grove and left them lying on the ground.

When Yamen saw them in the morning, he cried. And Grandpa sat by their cut trunks for a long time without speaking.

Then Grandpa got up, brushed the dust off his clothes, and said, "Yamen, a tree can be cut down, but its roots stay in the ground. And so do we."

Then he walked to the village.

The men of the village gathered in the square, old and young, and said, "The grove belongs to all of us, and the land belongs to all of us."

They agreed to take turns keeping watch over the groves at night, so that no land would be left without a guard.

So every night the men kept watch at the edges of the groves, with lanterns and copies of the Quran, taking turns until dawn.

Yamen brought them tea and bread, and heard them reciting: ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا اصْبِرُوا وَصَابِرُوا وَرَابِطُوا﴾

Standing guard was patience: the cold of the night, eyes kept awake, and fear that did not show on their faces.

But when the strangers saw the whole village staying awake to protect its land, they did not come back on those nights.

In the spring, the people of the village brought little olive seedlings and planted them where the cut trees had stood. Yamen planted one of them with his own hand.

Grandpa said, "This one is for your children, Yamen."

The years went by, and the seedling grew, and Yamen told its story to everyone who asked about it.

Land is only kept safe by its own people — when they are patient with it, stand firm on it, and never leave it.

﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا اصْبِرُوا وَصَابِرُوا وَرَابِطُوا وَاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ لَعَلَّكُمْ تُفْلِحُونَ﴾

📖 Al 'Imran 200. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

hijra.x:
For thirteen years, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called his people in Makkah to worship Allah alone, and they hurt him and hurt his Companions.

Then Allah allowed the Muslims to emigrate to Madinah. They left for it secretly, one after another, leaving behind their homes and their wealth.

The leaders of Quraysh gathered and agreed to kill the Prophet ﷺ. At night they stood at his door, waiting for him to come out.

But he walked out right past them, and they did not see him. He set off with his companion Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him).

The two of them hid in a cave in Mount Thawr for three nights.

Asma', the daughter of Abu Bakr, brought them food at night. When she could not find anything to tie it with, she tore her nitaq — a cloth belt — in two, and so she was called "Dhat an-Nitaqayn," the one with two belts.

Quraysh went out searching for them everywhere, and offered a big reward of camels to whoever brought them back.

The searchers even came and stood at the very mouth of the cave.

Abu Bakr said, "O Messenger of Allah, if one of them looked down at his feet, he would see us."

He ﷺ said, "What do you think, Abu Bakr, of two when Allah is the third of them?"

﴿إِذْ يَقُولُ لِصَاحِبِهِ لَا تَحْزَنْ إِنَّ اللَّهَ مَعَنَا﴾

No one saw them, and the searchers went back disappointed.

Then the two of them set out for Madinah along a different path from the usual road, with a guide who knew the desert.

Suraqah ibn Malik chased after them on his horse, hoping for the reward. But when he came close to them, his horse's legs sank into the sand, again and again.

He realised that they were being protected, so he turned back, and began turning other people away from their path.

The people of Madinah had heard that he had set out. Every morning they went out to the Harrah — an area covered with black stones — and waited for him until the sun grew hot.

Then they went back, and came out again the next day.

Until one day a man shouted from the top of a tall house: "Here he is — the one you've been waiting for has come!"

All the people of Madinah came out joyfully, old and young, to welcome the Prophet ﷺ and those with him.

The Muslims built a masjid in Madinah. And the Prophet ﷺ made brothers of the Muhajirun, who had left their homes, and the Ansar, the people of Madinah — who shared their homes and their wealth with them.

﴿وَالَّذِينَ تَبَوَّءُوا الدَّارَ وَالْإِيمَانَ مِن قَبْلِهِمْ يُحِبُّونَ مَنْ هَاجَرَ إِلَيْهِمْ﴾

📖 The story of the Hijrah is in Surat At-Tawbah, verse 40, and in Sahih Al-Bukhari. The last verse is from Surat Al-Hashr, verse 9.

dayn.x:
Uncle Munir was the neighbourhood baker. He baked every morning at dawn, and people bought their hot bread from him.

Tamim passed his bakery every morning on his way to school, and Uncle Munir would give him a little ka'k biscuit and say, "Here — to give you strength for your lessons."

Uncle Munir had borrowed money from Tamim's father, Hajj Rashid, to fix his oven when it broke down, and he had promised to pay it back at the end of the year.

When the end of the year came, he came to Hajj Rashid with his head bowed.

He said, "Hajj, business was slow this year, and my wife fell ill. I only have half the money. Please give me more time."

Hajj Rashid said, "The money is mine, and I've already given you a whole year." There was anger in his voice.

Uncle Munir left, sad. Tamim had heard everything.

The next morning he passed by the bakery and found Uncle Munir baking alone, his face tired — and he did not give him a ka'k.

When Tamim came back from school, he said to his father, "Baba, Uncle Munir has given me a ka'k every day for years, and he's never once taken money for it."

Then he said, "Shouldn't we give him back what he gave us?"

Hajj Rashid was quiet. Then he took out the mushaf and recited: ﴿وَإِن كَانَ ذُو عُسْرَةٍ فَنَظِرَةٌ إِلَىٰ مَيْسَرَةٍ ۚ وَأَن تَصَدَّقُوا خَيْرٌ لَّكُمْ﴾

And he said, "It means: if the person in debt is poor, give him time until he is able to pay. And if you let him off his debt, that is better for you."

Then he said, "And the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Whoever makes things easy for someone in hardship, Allah will make things easy for him in this world and the Hereafter.'"

Tamim said, "So will Allah make things easy for us if we make things easy for him?" His father said, "That is Allah's promise."

In the morning Hajj Rashid and Tamim went to the bakery. When Uncle Munir saw them, he was afraid and said, "Hajj, I haven't collected the rest yet."

Hajj Rashid said, "I've come to tell you: the half you gave me — take it for your wife's medicine. And as for the rest, I've let it go."

Uncle Munir cried and made a long du'a for them.

Then he took a big, hot ka'k out of the oven, split it between Tamim and his father, and said, "This one isn't for sale."

That year, business in Hajj Rashid's shop grew so much that he was amazed. And Tamim would say, "That's Allah's promise, Baba."

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever makes things easy for someone in hardship, Allah will make things easy for him in this world and the Hereafter."

📖 Narrated by Muslim. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

asir.x:
Long ago, Murad was a fisherman in a village by the sea. He went out in his boat every morning at dawn and came back before sunset.

Every evening his son Yasin waited for him on a rock by the shore.

One day Murad took his fish to the market in the city across the sea — and did not come back.

Then, days later, the news came: some goods had been stolen from a merchant at the port, and the guards had taken Murad and some other fishermen and locked them up unjustly. They had stolen nothing.

Yasin cried and said to Sheikh Bashir, the imam of the masjid, "My father has never taken anything that belongs to someone else!"

The Sheikh said, "I know that. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Free the captive.' Whoever is locked up unjustly is a captive, and freeing him is a right he has over all the Muslims — not only over his own family."

After Jumu'ah prayer, the Sheikh stood up and spoke to the people about the prisoners. He said, "We will send trustworthy men to the judge of the city to tell the truth as witnesses, and we will feed the prisoners' families until they come back."

Then he put a wooden box by the door of the masjid.

People came with whatever they had: one with some coins, another with his ring, another with a goat he had sold at the market.

Then a fisherman who had been out at sea with Murad on the day of the theft stood up and said, "I have no money, but I saw him on his boat with my own eyes. I will go with you and be a witness."

Yasin went to his little box where he had been saving his coins for years, to buy a fishing knife like his father's.

He looked at the coins for a long time. Then he carried all of them to the masjid.

When Sheikh Bashir saw him putting his coins in the box, he said, "Yasin, this is your money."

Yasin said, "And that is my father — and his brothers who are with him."

The trustworthy men sailed to the city, and the witness went with them. They stood before the judge and told him what they had seen. The judge asked questions until he found the real thief, and he ordered the fishermen to be set free.

And every evening Yasin stood on his rock, looking out at the sea.

One evening a white sail appeared far away. As it came closer, Yasin saw his father standing at the front of the ship, waving to him.

Yasin ran along the shore until his clothes were soaking wet.

When the captives came ashore, Murad hugged his son for a long time. Then he walked to the masjid and thanked the people of the village one by one.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Free the captive, feed the hungry, and visit the sick."

📖 Narrated by Al-Bukhari. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

haja.x:
Iyad had a little blue bike with a basket on the front, and he rode it around the neighbourhood every afternoon.

Their neighbour, Grandma Safiyya, lived alone in the house next door. She walked with a stick and hardly ever went out.

One day Iyad saw her walking to the corner shop in the heat: one step, then a stop, then another step.

When she came back, she was carrying a heavy bag, with her other hand on her stick.

Iyad ran to her and said, "Give me the bag, Grandma." He put it in his bike basket and walked beside her all the way to her door.

She made du'a for him and said, "May Allah help you, Iyad, as you have helped me."

When Iyad got home, he asked his father, "What does 'May Allah help you as you have helped me' mean?"

His father said, "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Whoever helps his brother with what he needs, Allah will help him with what he needs.'"

Then he said, "It means: when you go out of your way to help someone else with what they need, Allah takes care of what you need."

Iyad said, "Then I'll help Grandma Safiyya with what she needs every single day!"

So every afternoon Iyad knocked on her door and said, "What do you need from the shop, Grandma?"

He brought her bread and milk, took out her rubbish bag for her, and watered her plants if she forgot.

The shopkeeper would say, "I see you every day, Iyad, but you never buy anything for yourself!"

Iyad would laugh and say, "I'm shopping for my grandma."

One day Iyad's bike went missing. He had left it by the shop door, and when he came out, it was gone.

He searched the whole neighbourhood for it until Maghrib, then sat on the doorstep and cried.

Grandma Safiyya came out and asked him what was wrong. Then she raised her hands and made a long du'a for him.

In the morning, the shopkeeper came pushing the little blue bike and said, "My son found it near the market and recognised it by its basket. The whole neighbourhood knows Iyad's bike."

Iyad looked at Grandma Safiyya, remembered what his father had said — and understood.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever helps his brother with what he needs, Allah will help him with what he needs."

📖 Agreed upon (Al-Bukhari and Muslim). This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

surur.x:
Wa'il broke his leg in a football match, and he had to stay in hospital for weeks.

Muhannad sat next to him in class. Now Wa'il's seat was empty, and the class was quiet without his laugh.

Muhannad said to his mother, "I want to visit Wa'il, but I don't know what to say to him."

She said, "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'The deed most loved by Allah is joy that you bring to a Muslim.' So think: what would make him happy?"

Muhannad thought for a long time. Wa'il loves football, he loves laughing, and he loves the class team.

So at break time he gathered the boys in the class and said, "I've got an idea."

The boys made a big poster. Each of them drew himself on it and wrote Wa'il a short message.

In the middle of the poster they drew a goal with a ball in it, and under it: "We're waiting for you, goalie!"

Then they collected some of their pocket money and bought a new football, and each of them wrote his name on it.

And Muhannad said, "I'll bring him our lessons every day, so he doesn't fall behind."

They went to the hospital with their teacher. When they came into the room, Wa'il lifted his head in surprise. Then he saw the poster and laughed so loudly that people in the corridor could hear.

Then they gave him the ball. He turned it over in his hands, reading the names one by one, and then hugged it to his chest.

He said, "I didn't think you'd remember me."

The nurse said to the teacher, "This is the first day he's eaten all his food since he came here."

And every day Muhannad brought him the lessons and told him what had happened in class, and they laughed together.

When Wa'il left the hospital and came back to class on crutches, all the boys stood up and clapped.

Wa'il said, "It wasn't just the medicine that made me better. What made me better was that you made me happy."

Afterwards, Muhannad would say, "I've never been as happy in my life as I was the day Wa'il laughed."

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The deed most loved by Allah is joy that you bring to a Muslim."

📖 Narrated by At-Tabarani, and graded good (hasan) by Al-Albani. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

talut.x:
A long time after Musa (peace be upon him), an enemy defeated the Children of Israel. It drove them out of their homes and separated them from their children.

So their leaders came to a prophet who lived among them and said to him: ﴿ابْعَثْ لَنَا مَلِكًا نُّقَاتِلْ فِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ﴾

Their prophet said to them: ﴿هَلْ عَسَيْتُمْ إِن كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمُ الْقِتَالُ أَلَّا تُقَاتِلُوا﴾

He knew that talking is easy, but standing in front of the enemy is hard.

They said: ﴿وَمَا لَنَا أَلَّا نُقَاتِلَ فِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ وَقَدْ أُخْرِجْنَا مِن دِيَارِنَا وَأَبْنَائِنَا﴾

He said to them: ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ قَدْ بَعَثَ لَكُمْ طَالُوتَ مَلِكًا﴾

They were surprised and said, "How can he be king over us when he doesn't have much money?"

He said: ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ اصْطَفَاهُ عَلَيْكُمْ وَزَادَهُ بَسْطَةً فِي الْعِلْمِ وَالْجِسْمِ﴾

A leader needs knowledge and strength, not money.

Talut set out with the soldiers on a hot day. The road was long, and they grew more and more thirsty.

When they came near a river, he said to them: ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ مُبْتَلِيكُم بِنَهَرٍ فَمَن شَرِبَ مِنْهُ فَلَيْسَ مِنِّي وَمَن لَّمْ يَطْعَمْهُ فَإِنَّهُ مِنِّي إِلَّا مَنِ اغْتَرَفَ غُرْفَةً بِيَدِهِ﴾

When they reached the water, most of them rushed to it and drank until they were full.

﴿فَشَرِبُوا مِنْهُ إِلَّا قَلِيلًا مِّنْهُمْ﴾

But a few of them took just one handful of water in their hand, then stood up and left the river.

If someone cannot be patient about a drink of water, how will he be patient in front of the enemy?

Talut crossed the river with the few who had been patient. When they saw the army of Jalut (Goliath), they saw more soldiers than anyone could count, and among them Jalut, a huge man wearing iron armor.

Some of them said: ﴿لَا طَاقَةَ لَنَا الْيَوْمَ بِجَالُوتَ وَجُنُودِهِ﴾

Then those who knew they would meet Allah stood up and said to their brothers:

﴿كَم مِّن فِئَةٍ قَلِيلَةٍ غَلَبَتْ فِئَةً كَثِيرَةً بِإِذْنِ اللَّهِ ۗ وَاللَّهُ مَعَ الصَّابِرِينَ﴾

Victory is not counted by heads; it comes from Allah.

When they went out to face Jalut and his soldiers, they did not ask for weapons first. Instead, they raised their hands to Allah:

﴿رَبَّنَا أَفْرِغْ عَلَيْنَا صَبْرًا وَثَبِّتْ أَقْدَامَنَا وَانصُرْنَا عَلَى الْقَوْمِ الْكَافِرِينَ﴾

They asked for patience before victory, and for steady feet before winning.

Then Jalut came out, calling for someone to fight him one on one. The scholars of tafsir say that Dawud (peace be upon him) was a young man in Talut's army that day. He had a sling and some stones. He threw a stone at Jalut, and Jalut fell.

﴿فَهَزَمُوهُم بِإِذْنِ اللَّهِ وَقَتَلَ دَاوُودُ جَالُوتَ﴾

After that, Allah gave Dawud kingship and prophethood, and the people returned to their homes and their children.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿وَلَوْلَا دَفْعُ اللَّهِ النَّاسَ بَعْضَهُم بِبَعْضٍ لَّفَسَدَتِ الْأَرْضُ﴾

If the people of truth did not push back the wrongdoers, wrongdoing would fill the earth.

📖 Their story is in Surat Al-Baqarah, verses 246–251.

ghulaman.x:
In Madinah there were two boys from the Ansar, and each of them was named Mu'adh: Mu'adh ibn Amr and Mu'adh ibn Afra'.

They used to hear that Abu Jahl in Makkah insulted the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and tortured the weak Muslims, and this made them angry.

Then Quraysh set out with a big army against the Muslims, and Abu Jahl was in it.

The Muslims went out to meet them and camped at Badr. They had fewer men and fewer weapons. The two boys went out with them, each with his sword.

When the Muslims lined up in rows, Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf stood in the row. He looked to his right and to his left, and found himself between two young boys.

He wished he were between two men stronger than them, who would stand by him if the fighting became hard.

One of them nudged him secretly and said, "Uncle, do you know Abu Jahl?"

He said, "Yes. What do you want with him, my nephew?"

He said, "I was told that he insults the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. By the One in whose hand my soul is, if I see him, I will not leave him until whichever of us is meant to die first dies."

Abd al-Rahman was amazed at what the boy said.

Then the other boy nudged him from the other side and said the same thing as his friend, and neither of them had heard the other.

Soon Abd al-Rahman saw Abu Jahl moving among the people, with men around him guarding him.

He said to the two boys, "There he is — the man you asked me about."

The two boys rushed toward him. They were not stopped by how young they were, or by the men around him, or by the fact that he was the chief of Quraysh.

They struck him with their swords until they killed him.

Then they came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and told him. He said, "Which of you killed him?" Each of them said, "I killed him."

He said, "Have you wiped your swords?" They said, "No." He looked at the two swords and said, "You both killed him."

Allah gave the Muslims victory that day, even though they were few.

﴿وَلَقَدْ نَصَرَكُمُ اللَّهُ بِبَدْرٍ وَأَنتُمْ أَذِلَّةٌ﴾

And Abd al-Rahman realized that the two boys he had wished were stronger had the strongest hearts of all.

Strength is not in being tall or old. It is in a heart that becomes angry for Allah's sake and steps forward when others hold back.

📖 Agreed upon (Al-Bukhari and Muslim).

sahm.x:
Every morning, Sanad stood on the village wall, watching the young men train in the square at archery and horse riding.

What he wanted most was to be with them — and he was ten years old.

One day news came: a group of attackers was raiding the villages near the border, taking the sheep and burning the crops.

So the men and young men of the village got ready to go out to them and drive them away from the land.

Sanad ran to his father and said, "Take me with you, Father! I know how to shoot!"

His father stroked his head and said, "You are young, Sanad. War is for grown-ups."

So Sanad sat sadly by the door, watching the men prepare their swords while he had nothing to prepare.

Then Mays, the neighbors' daughter, who was memorizing Quran at the kuttab, came to him and said, "Why are you sad?"

He said, "They are all going out in the path of Allah except me."

She said, "Haven't you heard the hadith? The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Whoever equips a fighter has fought, and whoever looks after a fighter's family well while he is away has fought.'"

Sanad said, "What does 'equip' mean?"

She said, "It means giving him what he needs for his journey. And looking after his family means taking care of what his family needs until he comes back."

Sanad got up from where he was sitting. Now he knew what to do.

Layth was the youngest of the young men going out, and the poorest. He had nothing but an old bow and a few arrows.

So Sanad went to his box, took out the coins he had saved, bought a bundle of arrows with them, and carried it to Layth.

Mays came with a bag of dates and dry bread that her mother had sewn, and said, "This is for your journey, Layth."

Layth took it and said, "May Allah reward you both with good. Your arrows will be with me, Sanad, and your food, Mays."

When the men had gone, Sanad went every morning to Umm Layth's house. He carried water for her from the well and took her sheep out to graze with his father's sheep.

And Mays brought her bread whenever her own mother baked.

After some days, the men came back to the village. They had driven the attackers away from the border.

Layth got off his horse, came to Sanad, took an arrow out of his quiver, and said, "This is the last arrow left of the ones you gave me. Keep it. You were with us, Sanad."

Sanad hung the arrow above his bed. He looked at it every night and knew that he had not just stayed at home.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever equips a fighter in the path of Allah has fought, and whoever looks after a fighter's family well in the path of Allah has fought."

📖 Agreed upon (Al-Bukhari and Muslim). This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

baydar.x:
In the plain of Hauran there was a village of black stone, surrounded by fields of wheat. That year the rain came at the right time, and the wheat grew so tall that it covered the boys when they walked into it.

When harvest came, Abu Amjad's threshing floor had the highest pile of all. Amjad climbed to the top of it and shouted to the boys, "Look! Our pile is higher than your houses!"

One of the boys said to him, "May Allah bless it for you."

Amjad said as he climbed down, "That's because Allah loves us more than everyone else. Can't you see? He gave us what He didn't give you."

The boys went quiet, and none of them knew what to say.

In the village there was a boy named Ma'n. His father had died when he was little, so he and his mother walked behind the harvesters, picking up the ears of wheat that fell.

Ma'n came close to Abu Amjad's threshing floor to pick up grains scattered on the ground, and Amjad shouted at him, "Go away, Ma'n! This is our wheat!" Ma'n got up and left without saying a word.

Then Abu Amjad's storeroom filled up with sacks of wheat. Every evening Amjad counted them and felt happy.

In winter, Ma'n knocked on the door and said, "My mother says: Will you sell us a measure of flour? We will pay you after the harvest." Amjad said, "We have nothing to sell," and shut the door. His father was not at home.

When spring came, the fields turned green, and the people of the village were happy with their crops.

Then one afternoon the sky grew dark, and hail came down, white stones the size of chickpeas. It beat down on the hillside where Abu Amjad's field was, and passed lightly over the other fields.

When the sky was calm again, Amjad went out to the field with his father. The ears of wheat lay broken in the mud.

His father stood for a long time without speaking. Then he said, "Praise be to Allah in every situation," and went back home.

Amjad sat on the stone wall crying, and said to himself, "Allah is angry with us. He honored us last year, and He has humiliated us this year."

Then Ma'n came and sat beside him. He took a small loaf of bread out of his pocket, broke it in two, and gave him half.

Amjad looked at the bread and didn't take it. He said, "Didn't I chase you away from the threshing floor?"

Ma'n said, "When my father died, I thought Allah didn't love me. Then my mother said to me: Ma'n, Allah gives and holds back to see what we will do. Being rich is a test, and being poor is a test."

Amjad took the half loaf and was quiet. He remembered the sacks of wheat he used to count, and the door he had shut.

Then he went to his father and told him everything. His father said, "There is some left in the storeroom from last year. Carry a sack of it to Umm Ma'n, as a gift, not for sale." Amjad carried it on his back and hurried off.

When harvest came the next year, Amjad left the edge of the field uncut and said to Ma'n, "This is for you and your mother."

﴿فَأَمَّا الْإِنسَانُ إِذَا مَا ابْتَلَاهُ رَبُّهُ فَأَكْرَمَهُ وَنَعَّمَهُ فَيَقُولُ رَبِّي أَكْرَمَنِ ۝ وَأَمَّا إِذَا مَا ابْتَلَاهُ فَقَدَرَ عَلَيْهِ رِزْقَهُ فَيَقُولُ رَبِّي أَهَانَنِ ۝ كَلَّا ۖ بَل لَّا تُكْرِمُونَ الْيَتِيمَ ۝ وَلَا تَحَاضُّونَ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ﴾

📖 Al-Fajr 15–18. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

🌿 Reflection

The Quran names two mistaken ideas together: that being rich is a sign that Allah is pleased with you, and that being poor is a sign that He is angry with you.

In Surat al-Fajr, Allah answers anyone who measures His love by how much of this world they own with a single word: ﴿كَلَّا﴾ (“No indeed!”) — plenty and hardship are both a test, not an honour and not a humiliation.

The real measure is this: Did you honour the orphan? Did you encourage others to feed the poor? Or did love of money distract you from all of that?

qidr.x:
In Sheikha's house there was a big copper pot that her mother had inherited from her grandmother, and there was no other pot like it in the whole neighbourhood.

Whenever someone had a wedding, or guests, or Eid, they would knock on the door and say, "Lend us the big pot."

Sheikha was the one who carried it to whoever asked for it. Then she would bring it back black from the fire, and sit with her mother scrubbing it with sand until it shone.

One day, as she scrubbed, she said, "Our pot is in every house except ours!"

One day at noon, the pearl-diving ships came back to the shore. Ghanem, the neighbours' boy, ran to Sheikha's house and said, "My father is back, and the men from the ship are with him. My mother says: lend us the big pot."

Sheikha looked at the pot shining in the corner of the house. She had worked so hard scrubbing it the day before.

She said, "My mother is asleep, and I won't give it without her permission." But she knew her mother had never once turned anyone away.

Then she shut the door, went back to the pot, and sat down beside it.

A little later, Sheikha went up to the roof. In the neighbours' house she saw Umm Ghanem cooking rice in three small pots, putting them on the fire one after another, while the men waited in the sitting room.

The rice burned in one of them. Sheikha came down from the roof, and she did not look at the big pot.

When the sun began to go down, her mother woke up and found that the fire in the stove had gone out. She said, "Sheikha, take the little clay fire-pan and bring an ember from Umm Ghanem's house."

Sheikha stood at the door, then walked slowly to the neighbours' house, as if her feet did not want to walk.

Ghanem opened the door. When he saw the fire-pan in her hand, he took it and went inside. Then he came back with red embers in it, and with a plate of rice and fish too.

He said, "This is from the guests' lunch. My mother sent it for your mother."

Sheikha did not take the plate. She said in a quiet voice, "I'm the one who kept the pot from you, Ghanem."

Ghanem said, "I know. But an ember doesn't make our fire any smaller." Then he laughed and said, "And the pot wouldn't have got any smaller if it had cooked at our house for one day."

Sheikha took the fire-pan and the plate, went home and lit the fire, and told her mother everything.

Then she got up, carried the big pot to Umm Ghanem's house, and said, "Keep it as long as your guests are with you. When they leave, I'll come and carry it back."

Then Eid came, and the big pot went round every house in the neighbourhood, and each time Sheikha carried it without complaining.

﴿فَوَيْلٌ لِّلْمُصَلِّينَ ۝ الَّذِينَ هُمْ عَن صَلَاتِهِمْ سَاهُونَ ۝ الَّذِينَ هُمْ يُرَاءُونَ ۝ وَيَمْنَعُونَ الْمَاعُونَ﴾

📖 Al-Ma'un 4–7. The commentators mention that al-ma'un is what people lend one another, such as the pot, the bucket and the axe. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.

safwan.x:
Waddah lived in a village on a mountain. Its fields were like steps, one above the other. And he loved to hear people say, "How generous Waddah is!"

Whenever his father picked the grapes, Waddah carried a basket to the masjid courtyard after the prayer, where the men sat, and called out loudly, "Help yourselves! These grapes are from our house!"

One day his sister Arwa gave him a basket and said, "Take it to Uncle Mutahhar. He is a very old man who cannot see, and he never leaves his house."

Uncle Mutahhar's house was at the far end of the village, on a path where nobody ever walked. Waddah looked at the empty path, then he looked at the courtyard.

So he walked to the courtyard and handed out the grapes to the men until the basket was empty. They said, "May Allah bless you, Waddah! How generous you are!"

He went home happy, and he did not tell Arwa where he had taken the basket.

In the evening he sat with the boys by the well and told them what the men had said. Then he told it again to those who came after them, and then to everyone he met on the way.

His friend Nashwan listened and said nothing. In his hand was an empty jar.

On the way to the fields there was a big smooth rock. The wind had gathered a little soil on top of it, and green grass had grown in it.

Waddah said to Nashwan, "Look! The rock is greener than your father's field!" Nashwan said, "Its green is on top of stone. It has no roots to hold it."

Early in the morning, Waddah saw Nashwan climbing the empty path with a jar of water to Uncle Mutahhar's house, so he followed him.

He said, "Why tire yourself out here? Nobody can see you!" Nashwan said, "Uncle Mutahhar gets to drink, and Allah sees me. Isn't that enough?"

That night heavy rain fell, and Waddah heard the water running down the mountain until morning.

When the sun came up, he went out with Nashwan and Arwa. They passed the rock — and it was smooth and clean, with no soil on it and not a single blade of grass. But the fields below it were greener than before.

Arwa said, "In Surat Al-Baqarah there is a parable about someone who gives his wealth so that people will see him." Then she recited:

﴿فَمَثَلُهُ كَمَثَلِ صَفْوَانٍ عَلَيْهِ تُرَابٌ فَأَصَابَهُ وَابِلٌ فَتَرَكَهُ صَلْدًا﴾

She said, "Safwan is a smooth stone, wabil is very heavy rain, and sald is something smooth with nothing left on it."

Waddah stood in front of the rock for a long time. He remembered the men in the courtyard, then he said, "My grapes were soil on a stone."

Nashwan said, "And the rain did not take away the soil of the fields, because it is deep and the roots hold it. And Uncle Mutahhar is still waiting for his grapes."

In the afternoon Waddah carried a basket along the empty path. He sat with Uncle Mutahhar and handed him the grapes one by one, and the old man prayed for him.

When he came back, the boys by the well asked him, "Where were you?" He almost told them, then he said, "I had something to do." And in his heart was a joy he had never known before.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever does good deeds so that people will hear about them, Allah will let people hear what he really intended; and whoever does good deeds to be seen, Allah will show people what he really is."

📖 Agreed upon (Al-Bukhari and Muslim). This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.
